about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report to congressional committees examines (1) the changes and challenges described in the fiscal year 2009 overseas master plans, the extent to which they address prior GAO recommendations, and the plans' timeliness and (2) the status of DOD's master planning efforts for the proposed military buildup of forces and infrastructure on Guam. It is the fifth report responding to the fiscal year 2004 Senate military construction appropriation bill requirements and the second responding to the fiscal year 2007 requirements on Guam, and it is the final report to fulfill the congressional mandates.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The fiscal year 2009 overseas master plans generally reflect recent changes in U.S. overseas basing strategies and the challenges DOD faces in implementation, and they address most of GAO's prior recommendations, but DOD provided the plans to Congress in May 2008, 3 months after the February 2008 budget submission, rather than with the military construction budget submission as directed. The U.S. Pacific Command plan does not describe the Air Force's training challenges in South Korea despite GAO's prior recommendation that it do so. DOD has established a framework for the military buildup on Guam but has not issued the congressionally required comprehensive master plan, which was initially due December 2006 and extended to September 15, 2008; the working-level plan being developed is a onetime snapshot and is not considered a master plan. A comprehensive master plan is not expected until after the environmental impact statement and record of decision are completed, currently expected in December 2009 and January 2010, respectively. DOD has not fully addressed funding requirements, operational and training challenges, and impacts on Guam's community and public infrastructure.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The document reports the following figures: about 8,000 Marines and their estimated 9,000 dependents are to move from Okinawa, Japan, to Guam by 2014; Guam's current population of 171,000 is estimated to increase by approximately 25,000 active duty military personnel and dependents, or 14.6 percent, to 196,000; the total cost of all services' realignments on Guam is estimated to be more than $13 billion; the Marine Corps buildup is estimated to cost $10.3 billion and more recently was estimated by Marine Forces Pacific officials to exceed $15 billion; the government of Japan is expected to contribute a total of $6.09 billion, of which up to $2.8 billion would be in funds without reimbursement and another $3.3 billion in loans and equity investments; training ranges for the Marine Corps in Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands are estimated to cost $2 billion; strategic lift operating from Guam is estimated to cost an additional $88 million annually compared with operations from Okinawa; the U.S. European Command plan identified over $284 million in facility requirements for the ballistic missile defense program in the Czech Republic; the U.S. Central Command plan identified a goal of $1.7 billion in host nation funding; funding for the Japanese Facilities Improvement Program decreased from an estimated $1 billion in 1993 to $242 million; U.S. Forces Japan is returning more than 14,000 acres of land on Japan and Okinawa; U.S. Pacific Command is reducing major U.S. installations in South Korea from 41 to 10, or 76 percent; U.S. Army Europe returned nearly 20,000 soldiers and their families to the United States; the fiscal year 2009 military construction budget submission includes approximately $24.4 billion for military construction and family housing, of which nearly $1.1 billion, or 4.7 percent, is designated for specific overseas locations; the U.S. government has received approximately $656 million in residual value and payment-in-kind compensation since 1989; DOD officials estimate they will require 500 defense civilians and contractors to support Marine Corps base operations; preliminary analysis indicates 15,000 to 20,000 construction workers will be required and Guam may be able to meet only 10 to 15 percent of the labor requirement locally; a July 2008 study estimated annual construction capacity to be approximately $1 billion to $1.5 billion and potentially $2.5 billion with improvements to the port and road networks compared with an estimated construction capacity of more than $3 billion per year needed to meet the planned fiscal year 2014 completion date; the Governor of Guam testified that the government of Guam will need $6.1 billion for infrastructure upgrades; the military buildup may increase demand on Guam's water and wastewater systems by at least 25 percent; the ballistic missile defense task force would be approximately 630 soldiers and their estimated 950 dependents; the Navy issued a public notice of intent to prepare an environmental impact statement on March 7, 2007; and DOD submitted the fiscal year 2007 plans on April 27, the fiscal year 2008 plans on March 28, and the fiscal year 2009 plans in mid-May, 3 months after the fiscal year 2009 budget submission.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Secretary of Defense take two actions: direct the Under Secretary of Defense for Acquisition, Technology and Logistics to initiate a process of developing global defense posture updates earlier each year so that DOD can provide the congressional defense committees the overseas planning report with the administration's annual budget submission; and direct the Executive Director of the Joint Guam Program Office to provide the congressional defense committees with annual updates of the Guam working-level plan until a comprehensive master plan is finalized and submitted to Congress.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document does not settle the following: DOD has not identified all funding requirements for the Guam buildup, and the $13 billion estimate excludes the costs of all other defense organizations that will be needed; the Marine Corps realignment cost estimate has risen from $10.3 billion to over $15 billion; plans for the detailed force composition of units relocating to Guam, associated facility requirements, and implications for other services' realignments continue to be refined, including no decision on whether to deploy additional forces under the Grow the Force initiative; the environmental impact statement and record of decision are not expected to be completed until December 2009 and January 2010, respectively; DOD officials said the working-level plan will be a snapshot of the planning process and will not be considered a comprehensive master plan; the government of Japan's $6.09 billion contribution is conditional on its review and agreement to specific infrastructure plans and on progress of other initiatives; Guam's public infrastructure challenges and the $6.1 billion in funding the Governor said is needed have not been resolved; construction capacity is expected to be less than the more than $3 billion per year DOD needs; and no requirement exists to report periodically on the status of DOD's planning efforts for Guam after September 2008 until a comprehensive master plan is completed, currently expected no sooner than 2010.

audience.name: Who it is for
audience.text: The report is addressed to the congressional defense committees, including the Senate and House Committees on Armed Services and the defense and military construction appropriations subcommittees, to inform their decisions on defense appropriations and oversight.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a U.S. Government Accountability Office report to the House Committee on Foreign Affairs, issued August 28, 2008, examining the fate of exported used electronics, the effectiveness of U.S. regulatory controls over those exports (mainly EPA's cathode-ray tube rule under the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act), and opportunities for strengthening the federal role through stronger enforcement and more comprehensive regulation.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The document's findings are GAO's own, based on review of EPA documents, interviews with EPA, State Department, and Customs and Border Protection officials, Internet monitoring, and undercover exercises posing as foreign buyers. It finds that while some exported used electronics are handled responsibly, a substantial amount ends up in countries such as China and India where they are often handled and disposed of unsafely, including through open-air burning and acid baths. It finds that current U.S. regulatory controls do little to stem exports of potentially hazardous used electronics because the scope of regulation is narrow, covering only CRTs; the controls are easily circumvented; and EPA has done little to enforce the CRT rule. GAO found 43 U.S. electronics recyclers willing to export broken, untested, or nonworking CRTs under conditions that would appear to violate the CRT rule, and EPA records showed none of those recyclers had filed proper notifications. It also finds that Hong Kong intercepted and returned 26 containers of used CRT monitors, and EPA did not issue its first administrative penalty complaint until July 2008, after GAO identified a problem. The document concludes that EPA has established no enforcement targets, done no monitoring, conducted only preliminary follow-up, and taken only one enforcement action.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The document gives these figures: Americans removed more than 300 million electronic devices from their households in 2006; CRTs contain up to 4 pounds of lead; functional secondhand computers exported from the United States to Africa can be purchased for less than 1/10th the cost of a new one; the Basel Convention has been ratified by 170 countries; the agency's July 2006 CRT rule required notifications starting in January 2007; copper prices increased threefold over the last several years; GAO e-mailed 343 solicitations and 64 responded; over a 3-month period from mid-February to mid-May 2008, brokers in developing countries made 230 requests for about 7.5 million used CRTs; brokers in developing countries represented over 60 percent of all requests; over 75 percent of brokers' requests offered $10 or less per unit and almost half offered $5 or less; about 70 percent of requests came from developing countries in Asia; on one e-commerce site there were 2,234 requests for LCD screens, 430 for central processing units, and 665 for used computers; Samsung Corning's contractor coordinated with approximately 40 U.S. recyclers; about 250 shipping containers totaling about 4,000 tons of CRT glass leave the United States for Malaysia each month; Samsung Corning manufactures CRT televisions containing as much as 50 percent recycled-glass content; a United Nations University study found manufacturing takes up 80 percent of natural resources used during computers' life cycle; the U.S. Geological Survey reports 1 metric ton of computer scrap contains more gold than 17 metric tons of ore; more than 10,000 people work in Delhi's informal recycling industry; scavengers in Cambodia collect material for as little as $1 a day; functional used computers sell in West Africa for as little as $100; shipping rates from the United States to West Africa range from $4,000 to $7,000 per 20-foot container versus $750 for 40-foot containers to Hong Kong; an African importer can profit with up to 40 percent "junk"; as of June 2008, 25 companies had submitted 47 notices for export of CRTs for recycling; 43 U.S. companies were willing to export nonworking CRTs to GAO's fictitious buyers, 3 others said they do not export broken CRTs, and 7 asked for more information; one Maryland recycler charges $10 to $30 for CRT monitors; one Missouri recycler offered a 10 percent discount; a New York recycler made four purchases including 221 CRT monitors; a Georgia recycler bought 100 CRT monitors for $45 and 155 for $366 and offered three container-loads, raising loads from about 850 to between 1,100 and 1,200 monitors per container for an additional $400; Hong Kong intercepted and returned 26 containers of used CRT monitors; from January to July 2008, Hong Kong information covered six shipments (10 40-foot containers) of waste CRTs; three 40-foot containers were shipped across the Pacific four times, sat at port 11 more days, and were intercepted a second time about 3 weeks later; violations can bring criminal penalties of up to $50,000 per day and imprisonment of up to 2 years; EPA issued its first administrative penalty complaint in July 2008 seeking $32,500; as of August 2008, EPA reported 10 ongoing investigations, 7 of which appeared to be from GAO; children in Guiyu had lead levels more than 50 percent higher than the CDC limit and more than 50 percent higher than in a neighboring village; consumer electronics comprise less than two percent of the municipal solid waste stream; recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document recommends that the Administrator of EPA identify a timetable for developing and implementing a systematic plan to enforce the CRT rule, including enforcement targets, monitoring, follow-up of suspected violations, and prosecution. It also recommends that the Administrator direct appropriate offices to develop options under existing RCRA authority to broaden regulations for exported used electronic devices that are not classified as hazardous waste by current U.S. regulations but have a high likelihood of threatening human health and the environment when unsafely disassembled, considering expansion of the CRT rule and revision of the regulatory definition of hazardous waste; cooperate with other federal agencies to improve tracking of exported used electronics, which could be accomplished by implementing specific harmonized tariff codes; and submit to Congress a legislative package for ratification of the Basel Convention. The document notes that EPA generally disagreed with these recommendations.

It notes EPA had no plans and no timetable for developing an enforcement strategy for the CRT rule. The document also states that there are lingering uncertainties over the Basel Convention's definitions of exports for recycling, refurbishment, and reuse; that some Basel parties argue the convention regulates used products for repair, refurbishment, or remanufacture; that the U.S. State Department takes the position that trade of used products for refurbishment is not within the convention; and that the scrap-recycling industry has mixed views about Basel ratification. It notes that regulating used electronics exported for reuse could create an "overwhelming" number of notice-and-consent requests and could be managed only with additional resources. The document also notes that its figure on countries requesting CRTs assumes buyers do not post fictitious country names and that there is no double counting of requests.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is GAO report GAO-08-1075R, issued September 16, 2008, addressed to two House Homeland Security subcommittee chairmen. It identifies, for each of the 18 critical infrastructure sectors, the federal laws, regulations, and mandatory standards that pertain to securing privately owned information technology systems and data, and identifies enforcement mechanisms for each. It also transmits the July 24, 2008, briefing slides presented to congressional staff, and it excludes privately owned IT systems and data operated on behalf of a federal agency.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The GAO identified at least 34 federal laws, regulations, and mandatory standards for securing privately owned IT systems and data: 1 law, 25 regulations, and 8 mandatory standards, applying to 10 of the 18 critical infrastructure sectors. The drinking water and water treatment systems sector has the one law; the banking and finance sector has 17 regulations; and the dams and energy sectors share 8 mandatory standards. Eight sectors did not identify any such requirements: critical manufacturing, defense industrial base, emergency services, government facilities, information technology, national monuments and icons, postal and shipping, and telecommunications. Each of the 34 requirements has at least one enforcement mechanism, including court injunctions, civil monetary penalties, criminal penalties, and administrative actions, though these mechanisms are generally not specific to securing IT systems and data. The sector-specific agencies agreed with the information in the report.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The source gives these figures: Federal policy identifies 18 infrastructure sectors. The GAO identified at least 34 federal laws, regulations, and mandatory standards, consisting of 1 law, 25 regulations, and 8 mandatory standards, applying to 10 of the 18 sectors. The 8 sectors with no identified requirements are critical manufacturing, defense industrial base, emergency services, government facilities, information technology, national monuments and icons, postal and shipping, and telecommunications. By sector, the applicable counts are: agriculture and food, 1 regulation; banking and finance, 17 regulations; chemical, 1 regulation; commercial facilities, 1 regulation; dams, 8 mandatory standards; drinking water and water treatment systems, 1 law; energy, 1 regulation and 8 mandatory standards; nuclear reactors, materials, and waste, 1 regulation; public health and healthcare, 1 regulation; and transportation systems, 2 regulations. The dams and energy sectors share the same 8 mandatory standards, counted once in the 34. Enforcement figures stated include: a banking or finance civil monetary penalty of up to $1 million per day; a drinking water violation fine of up to $25,000 per violation; a nuclear regulation fine of up to $100,000 per day per violation; a chemical facility fine of up to $25,000 per day; a commercial facilities violation fine of up to $25,000 per violation; an agriculture and food penalty of imprisonment for up to one year, a fine of up to $1,000, or both; a public health and healthcare penalty of up to $50,000, imprisonment for up to 1 year, or both; and a transportation systems fine of up to $100,000 for each violation. The drinking water law applies to community water systems serving more than 3,300 people. The document also gives these dates and deadlines: a July 24, 2008 briefing; an October 2007 prior report; a September 2008 deadline for sector-specific agencies to develop plans; audit work performed from November 2007 to July 2008; and vulnerability assessment completion deadlines of March 31, 2003 for systems serving 100,000 or more people, December 31, 2003 for systems serving 50,000 or more but less than 100,000, and June 30, 2004 for systems serving more than 3,300 but less than 50,000.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document reports GAO's recommendation that the Secretary of Homeland Security request that, by September 2008, the sector-specific agencies develop plans that address all of the key aspects of cyber security in their sector-specific plans.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that the agencies may not have identified all applicable requirements and that GAO did not conduct an independent search for applicable requirements. It also states that the review did not include privately owned IT systems and data operated on behalf of a federal agency, including contractor-operated systems subject to the Federal Information Security Management Act of 2002. The enforcement mechanisms and authorities identified are examples and do not necessarily constitute a complete list, and the mechanisms are typically general enforcement tools rather than specific to securing privately owned IT systems and data. Where GAO could not reconcile its analysis with agencies' interpretations, it reported the agencies' characterizations. In addition, the chemical sector's risk-based performance standards have not been finalized or submitted to the Office of Management and Budget and are not yet enforceable.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a U.S. Government Accountability Office report to congressional requesters, issued September 11, 2008 (GAO-08-1078), assessing the Federal Aviation Administration's ability to acquire and integrate new air traffic control systems and transition to the Next Generation Air Transportation System (NextGen). Its scope covers three research questions: the status and outcome of FAA's ATC systems acquisition activities; the status of key NextGen planning and transition issues; and the key challenges FAA faces in implementing NextGen, including research and development, human capital, and infrastructure.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: Most of FAA's major ATC acquisition programs are being managed within established cost and schedule estimates since the creation of ATO in 2004: 24 major acquisition programs experienced a cumulative 2.5 percent cost underage and a 2.7 percent schedule overage when February 2004 baselines were compared with June 2008 estimates. JPDO completed initial versions of three basic NextGen planning documents, and ATO reorganized in May 2008, but stakeholders had concerns about their participation in planning, the usefulness of the planning documents, and the adequacy of FAA's management structure. FAA faces key challenges in implementing NextGen: uncertain research and development funding and research gaps, human capital and skills shortages, facility maintenance and reconfiguration, and airport capacity limits, with FAA analyses indicating 14 more airports will still need additional capacity by 2025. The report also found that FAA's performance measured against original baselines was lower than reported: acquisitions reported from 2003 to 2006 collectively exceeded original budget estimates by approximately $4.4 billion, or over 66 percent, with schedule slippages of from 1 to 10 years.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The report states that one in four flights faces delays; the U.S. system handles about 50,000 flights over a 24-hour period; by 2025 air traffic is projected to increase two-to-three-fold to about 100,000 to 150,000 flights every 24 hours; in 2007, 27 percent of flights were delayed or canceled; and delays cost passengers, airlines, and the U.S. economy over $40 billion. From February 2004 to June 2008, 24 major acquisition programs experienced a cumulative 2.5 percent cost underage and a cumulative 2.7 percent schedule overage; of the 24, 19 were at or less than baseline cost and 15 were at or earlier than baseline schedule. Acquisitions reported from 2003 to 2006 collectively exceeded original budget estimates by approximately $4.4 billion, or over 66 percent, and experienced schedule slippages of from 1 to 10 years. FAA plans to spend roughly $5.4 billion from fiscal years 2009 through 2013 on NextGen development and capital costs; the total federal cost for NextGen infrastructure through 2025 is estimated at $15 billion to $22 billion, with a corresponding cost to system users of $14 billion to $20 billion. NASA's aeronautics research budget in constant 2008 dollars was $986 million in 2003, $959 million in 2004, $906 million in 2005, $884 million in 2006, $594 million in 2007, $512 million in 2008, and a proposed $447 million in 2009, $448 million in 2010, $452 million in 2011, $457 million in 2012, and $468 million in 2013; the text also says the budget declined from about $959 million in 2004 to $511 million in 2008. FAA's overall research and development funding in constant 2008 dollars was $137 million in 2006, $237 million in 2007, $271 million in 2008, $337 million in 2009, $419 million in 2010, $431 million in 2012, and $436 million in 2013. FAA estimates it will spend $740 million on NextGen-related research and development during fiscal years 2009 through 2013; the proposed fiscal year 2009 budget requests $56.5 million for FAA research and development to support NextGen, compared with $24.3 million authorized for fiscal year 2008. Proposed legislation would allow $111 million for fiscal years 2009 through 2011 for the CLEEN program, and FAA plans to invest $180.4 million in human factors research from fiscal year 2009 to fiscal year 2013. FAA estimates it could need 150 to 200 more staff. FAA is responsible for maintaining over 400 terminal facilities, rated the average condition of 89 of them as fair, and estimated a one-time repair cost of $250 million to $350 million for all terminal facilities. FAA developed a rolling 10-year plan for capacity improvements at the nation's 35 busiest airports, and found that by 2025, 14 airports will still need additional capacity. The report also reports stakeholder response counts, including 21 of 22 stakeholders who discussed the issue felt they had the opportunity to participate, 13 of 15 who discussed the issue felt participation did not allow sufficient meaningful input, 19 of 21 who discussed the issue said planning documents lacked needed information, all 10 stakeholders who discussed FAA's 2007 management structure viewed it as not adequate, 13 of 15 who discussed leadership felt FAA did not have the leadership in place, and 11 of 12 who discussed a gradual rollout suggested FAA consider one.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document restates recommendations GAO made in prior work. In December 2007, GAO recommended that FAA identify or establish a vehicle for regularly reporting to Congress and the public on the agency's overall, long-term performance in acquiring ATC systems by providing original budget and schedule baselines for each rebaselined program and the reasons for the rebaselining, and that FAA report information on the potential effects that any budget increases or schedule slippages could have on the overall transition to NextGen. In November 2006, GAO recommended that FAA examine its strengths and weaknesses with regard to the technical expertise and contract management expertise that will be required to define, implement, and integrate the numerous complex programs inherent in the transition to NextGen. The report notes that FAA plans to address the December 2007 recommendation by reporting such information in its Capital Improvement Plan, which it sends annually to Congress.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report states that it is too early to tell whether ATO's May 2008 reorganization addresses stakeholder concerns about the fragmented management structure for NextGen, since other offices in ATO and FAA continue to have responsibility for parts of NextGen and the division of responsibility is not clear. It is also too early to tell whether the four research transition teams established by FAA and NASA will be effective in addressing NextGen's overall research needs. JPDO has not yet determined what NextGen research and development needs to be done first and at what cost to demonstrate and integrate NextGen technologies. FAA has not developed a cost analysis or implementation plan for reconfiguring its facilities, and until that analysis and plan are developed the configurations needed for NextGen cannot be implemented. NAPA expected to publish the second part of its skill-gap study in September 2008. It remains to be seen whether FAA's planned human factors research will offset NASA's reductions. FAA has not assessed the physical condition of all of its terminal facilities. The report also notes that the level of detail some stakeholders asked for, such as specifications to develop and manufacture NextGen equipment, will not be available for projects that are still in the concept development and investment analysis phase.

audience.text: The audience is the congressional requesters listed in the report, including the Chairman and Ranking Member of the House Committee on Science and Technology, the Ranking Republican Member of the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure, and the Chairman and Ranking Member of the Senate and House aviation subcommittees, for congressional oversight of FAA's ATC modernization and NextGen transition.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This U.S. Government Accountability Office report (GAO-08-1123, issued September 18, 2008) is addressed to congressional requesters and examines collaboration between the Small Business Administration (SBA) and USDA Rural Development in rural economic development. It covers (1) whether the complementary nature of some SBA and Rural Development loan and business programs provides a rationale for collaboration, (2) past and current collaborative efforts between SBA and Rural Development and between those agencies and other agencies, and (3) opportunities to facilitate more effective collaboration.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report finds that some SBA loan programs and Rural Development business programs are complementary, which provides a rationale for collaboration: they serve similar rural areas and borrowers, offer comparable products, and have different strengths, such as faster SBA processing times versus larger Rural Development loan amounts. The report also finds that collaborative efforts between SBA and Rural Development have been sporadic, mostly initiated at the local level, and dependent on established working relationships; the extent and formality of collaboration varied widely by location. A few offices, such as those in North Dakota, collaborated frequently and used formal mechanisms such as memorandums of understanding, while offices in many other states did not appear to be collaborating at all. The report finds that SBA and Rural Development lack a lasting formal approach to collaboration: a December 2000 memorandum of understanding expired in 2003, does not appear to have been implemented while active, and was not renewed, and the agencies do not have formal incentives or tracking of collaborative results. The report concludes that without a formal approach, the agencies are less likely to fully leverage each other's strengths to improve small business opportunities and promote economic development in rural communities.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: In fiscal year 2007, SBA's 7(a) program provided more than 99,000 loans totaling nearly $14 billion; the 504 program provided about 11,000 loans totaling approximately $6 billion; the 7(m) program provided about $19 million in microloans; and the Small Business Investment Company program provided over $2.5 billion in venture capital funding to more than 2,000 small businesses. In the same period, Rural Development's Business and Industry program provided over $836 million in loan guarantees; the Intermediary Relending Program totaled about $34 million; the Rural Business Enterprise Grant Program provided approximately $43 million in grants; the Rural Business Opportunity Grant Program provided about $7 million; the Rural Economic Development Loan and Grant Program provided about $26 million in loans and about $10 million in grants; and the Renewable Energy Systems and Energy Efficiency Improvements program provided approximately $48 million in energy loans, $11 million in energy grants, and over $18 million in joint funding. The Small/Rural Lender Advantage Pilot Program uses a simplified application for loans of $350,000 or less, with SBA guaranteeing 85 percent of loans up to $150,000 and 75 percent of loans above $150,000. The 7(m) program provides loans of up to $35,000, with an average loan size of about $13,000. SBA has 68 field offices, 63 lead Small Business Development Centers, and more than 1,000 satellite locations; Rural Development has 47 state offices and about 500 area or local field offices. The maximum SBA 7(a) loan is $2 million, compared with a maximum Business and Industry loan of $25 million; maximum guaranty percentages are 85 percent for 7(a) loans up to $150,000 and 75 percent above, while Business and Industry guaranties are 80 percent up to $5 million, 70 percent from $5 million to $10 million, and 60 percent above $10 million. SBA loan processing generally takes 5 to 7 business days, sometimes as little as 2 days for 7(a), while Rural Development processing takes 10 to 60 days. Rural Development programs generally serve areas with 50,000 or fewer people, except the Intermediary Relending Program, which serves areas with 25,000 or fewer. In North Dakota, officials estimated that about one of every four 504 loans in rural communities with populations under 25,000 had been used jointly with Intermediary Relending loans. The report also cites a $7.2 million SBA 504 loan for a health care business with 301 professionals, 760 daily patients, and annual sales over $9 million, and a $600,000 Rural Development Intermediary Relending award that assisted 7 businesses, created 200 jobs, and saved 259 jobs. USDA previously closed or consolidated about 1,500 county offices and transferred more than 600 field positions. About half of SBA's 68 district offices and about half of Rural Development's 47 state offices reported ongoing collaborative efforts. The December 2000 memorandum of understanding expired in 2003. The report also cites eight key practices for federal collaboration identified in its October 2005 report.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document recommends that the Administrator of SBA and the Secretary of Agriculture take steps to adopt a formal approach to encourage further collaboration in support of common economic development goals in rural areas. Such steps could include establishing and implementing a written agreement; defining and articulating a common outcome for rural economic development; specifying roles and responsibilities to ensure proper coordination; establishing mechanisms to monitor, evaluate, and report on results; and reinforcing accountability for collaborative efforts. The document makes no other recommendations.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that there is no commonly accepted definition of collaboration, so it defines the term for its own purposes. It also notes that collaboration between SBA and Rural Development is not specifically required by law or regulation. Its information on current collaborative efforts came from responses from about half of SBA's district offices and all of Rural Development's state offices, and from site visits to three locations selected to reflect a range of collaborative efforts. The report says SBA and Rural Development 'do not appear' to have implemented the December 2000 memorandum of understanding while it was active, and that the lack of implementation 'may' have been due to a change in USDA administration and a lack of monitoring. At the outset of the review, headquarters officials could not provide descriptions of joint efforts, and the agencies did not track the results of some collaborative efforts; for example, Rural Development officials in New Mexico had not been able to document a loan resulting from their 'Access to Capital' forums.

audience.text: The report is addressed to congressional requesters, specifically the Chairman and Ranking Member of the Senate Committee on Small Business and Entrepreneurship, the Chairman and Ranking Member of the House Subcommittee on Rural and Urban Entrepreneurship, and one additional House member, to support congressional oversight and decisions regarding whether and how SBA and USDA Rural Development collaboration could be improved.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) report, GAO-08-1138, issued September 17, 2008, titled Health Information Technology: HHS Has Taken Important Steps to Address Privacy Principles and Challenges, Although More Work Remains. It is a follow-up study of the Department of Health and Human Services' Office of the National Coordinator for Health Information Technology efforts to ensure the privacy of electronic personal health information exchanged within a nationwide health information network. The report updates whether the department has defined and implemented an overall privacy approach, as GAO recommended in January 2007, and examines HHS initiatives, plans, milestones, and stakeholder contributions related to privacy principles and challenges.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report's own findings are that, since January 2007, HHS has undertaken various initiatives contributing to an overall privacy approach and has fulfilled the first part of GAO's recommendation by identifying milestones and assigning to the Director of the Office of Policy and Research responsibility for integrating privacy-related outcomes and developing a confidentiality, privacy, and security framework. HHS has taken important steps on the other two parts, addressing HIPAA privacy principles and challenges to nationwide exchange, but has not fully implemented the recommendation because it has not defined a process for ensuring that all key privacy principles and challenges will be fully and adequately addressed. Examples of initiatives include the Healthcare Information Technology Standards Panel's security standards, the Certification Commission for Healthcare Information Technology's certification criteria with privacy protections, and state-level initiatives such as the Health Information Security and Privacy Collaboration and the State Alliance for e-Health. The June 2008 federal health IT strategic plan includes privacy and security objectives with strategies and target dates, and the Office of the National Coordinator expects to publish a confidentiality, privacy, and security framework by December 2008. In HHS's written comments, the department generally agreed with the draft report but neither agreed nor disagreed with GAO's recommendation, agreed that more work remains, and stated it is actively pursuing a two-phased process for assessing and prioritizing privacy-related initiatives.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The report is GAO-08-1138, issued September 17, 2008, and is 27 pages long. A September 2007 survey sponsored by the Institute of Medicine found that nearly 60 percent of respondents did not believe the privacy of personal medical records and health information was adequately protected by federal and state laws and organizational practices. President Bush issued Executive Order 13335 on April 27, 2004, calling for widespread adoption of interoperable electronic health records within 10 years; in 2004 the Secretary of HHS documented a health IT framework. In 2005, HHS awarded four health IT contracts that included requirements for developing solutions to comply with federal privacy requirements and identifying techniques and standards for securing health information. In January 2007, four test network implementations, or prototypes, demonstrated potential nationwide health information exchange. The State-Level Health Information Exchange Consensus Project issued a report in February 2007 and another in March 2008. The Confidentiality, Privacy, and Security Workgroup submitted recommendations related to the notice principle in February and April 2008. The National Committee on Vital and Health Statistics submitted five recommendations to the Secretary in February 2008. The State Alliance for e-Health's information protection task force proposed five recommendations in August 2007. The Secretary released the ONC-Coordinated Federal Health IT Strategic Plan: 2008-2012 on June 3, 2008; strategies include completing a confidentiality, privacy, and security framework by the end of 2008 and addressing inconsistent statutes or regulations by the end of 2011. The Office of the National Coordinator expects to publish the framework by December 2008. GAO conducted the performance audit from April 2008 through September 2008. HHS submitted written comments dated September 11, 2008. A footnote states HHS awarded contracts to nine health information exchange organizations and cooperative agreements to six additional organizations for trial implementations. HHS's comments set the goal that most Americans have secure electronic health records by 2014.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: This document recommends that the Secretary of Health and Human Services direct the National Coordinator for Health IT to include in the department's overall privacy approach a process for assessing and prioritizing its many privacy-related initiatives and the needs of stakeholders, so that key privacy principles and challenges are fully and adequately addressed. It also reiterates the January 2007 recommendation that HHS define and implement an overall approach for protecting health information that identifies milestones and the entity responsible for integrating privacy initiative outcomes, ensures key privacy principles in HIPAA are fully addressed, and addresses key challenges of nationwide health information exchange. HHS's comments state the department is actively pursuing a two-phased process for assessing and prioritizing privacy-related initiatives, but the department neither agreed nor disagreed with the recommendation.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report does not settle whether HHS's overall privacy approach will ensure comprehensive privacy protection; it states that HHS has not defined a process for ensuring that all privacy principles and challenges are fully and adequately addressed, and that without such a process some principles and challenges may receive inadequate attention, creating gaps. It notes that recommendations from the Confidentiality, Privacy, and Security Workgroup and the National Committee on Vital and Health Statistics were still under consideration by the Secretary. It also notes HHS's written comment that the report lists representative examples of HHS initiatives and is not a complete compilation of HHS's privacy and security activities, and GAO states HHS neither agreed nor disagreed with its recommendation.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This U.S. Government Accountability Office report, GAO-08-180, examines the limitations of first responders' tools for detecting and modeling chemical, biological, radiological, and nuclear (CBRN) hazardous releases in urban areas. It addresses four questions: the limitations of detection equipment, DHS's development and adoption of performance standards and its testing of equipment, the limitations of plume models for tracking urban airborne releases, and the information available on the effects of CBRN exposure on urban populations. The report was prepared for congressional requesters and covers work conducted from July 2004 to January 2008.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report finds that more than 6 years after the events of September 11, 2001, local first responders do not have tools that can accurately and quickly identify the release of CBRN material in an urban environment. Radiological and nuclear detection equipment can detect the presence of significant amounts of these materials but cannot predict their dispersion in the atmosphere, and no federal agency has a mission to develop, independently test, and certify radiological detection equipment for first responders' use in detecting atmospheric releases. Commercially available chemical and biological detectors cannot detect all agents and have varying sensitivity and specificity; according to DHS, chemical detectors are generally inadequate for detecting chemical warfare agents at less than lethal but still potentially harmful levels, and handheld immunoassays for biological threat agents have not passed acceptable standards for effectiveness. BioWatch does not provide real-time detection: identification and confirmation of biological agents can take several hours to more than a day after release, and the quantity released cannot be determined. DHS had adopted very few performance standards for CBRN detection equipment as of October 30, 2007, and it does not independently test and validate manufacturers' claims about commercial equipment. Nonurban plume models have significant limitations in complex urban settings and have not been adequately validated; TOPOFF 2 produced contradictory plume modeling results, TOPOFF 3 showed continuing coordination problems, and TOPOFF 4 showed improvement but decision makers had difficulty interpreting radiation dispersal predictions. Urban plume models have an unpredictable range of uncertainty and cannot determine the source term of a release with certainty. Significant data gaps exist on how CBRN releases affect urban populations, especially vulnerable populations, and dose-response parameters for the general population do not exist for most chemical warfare agents believed to pose a threat to civilians.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: In the sarin release scenario, it is estimated that 6,000 people are killed and economic damages amount to $300 million. The 2001 anthrax attacks resulted in 22 persons contracting anthrax disease and 5 deaths in four states and Washington, D.C. Approximately 800,000 shipments of hazardous materials travel daily throughout the United States. The 1984 Bhopal release killed approximately 3,800 people. In Graniteville, South Carolina, on January 6, 2005, 11,500 gallons of chlorine gas were released, causing 9 deaths, 8 from inhaling chlorine gas, and at least 529 people to seek medical care; 5,453 residents were evacuated. As of October 30, 2007, DHS had adopted 39 total standards for CBRN equipment, including 4 standards for radiation and nuclear detection instruments and none for chemical or biological detection equipment; the remaining standards address personal protective equipment. DHS spending for the BioWatch program during fiscal years 2005 to 2007 was about $236 million. BioWatch serves more than 30 jurisdictions and cannot identify a threat agent until several hours to more than a day after release, with a sample collection cycle of 24 hours. Handheld immunoassays yield results in approximately 15 minutes. DHS S&T assessed the sensitivity of ion mobility spectrometers and surface acoustic wave devices for V and G nerve agents at approximately 2 ppb to 20 ppb, while the limit of detection for blister agents such as mustard and lewisite is 200 ppb to 300 ppb; electrochemical cells can detect from ppb to low parts per million. Real-time detection has been defined as 30 seconds or less from the time potential material reaches the device until an alarm is triggered. In Seattle and Washington state, about $3.2 million of State Homeland Security Program and Urban Areas Security Initiative grant funds were used to acquire CBRN detection equipment in 2004-2005; Seattle alone spent about $500,000, and Connecticut spent about $1.8 million in DHS grants for CBRN detection equipment in 2003-2005. Washington State Radiation Protection officials found that one brand of digital dosimeters consistently read only 40 percent of what their current dosimeters and instruments read. As of October 2007, DHS's Responder Knowledge Base included 1,127 certifications for equipment on DHS's authorized equipment list and 268 reports of operational suitability testing of CBRN equipment. CAMEO/ALOHA includes emergency response information for over 6,000 chemicals and does not make predictions for distances greater than 6.2 miles (10 kilometers) from the release point or for more than an hour after a release begins. NARAC and IMAAC can provide an automated prediction for CBRN events within 5 to 15 minutes.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Secretary of Homeland Security reach agreement with DOD, DOE, EPA, and other agencies involved with developing, testing, and certifying CBRN detection equipment on which agency should have the missions and responsibilities to develop, independently test, and certify detection equipment that first responders can use to detect hazardous material releases in the atmosphere; ensure that manufacturers' claims are independently tested and validated regarding whether their commercial off-the-shelf CBRN detection equipment can detect given hazardous material at specific sensitivities; refine IMAAC's procedures by working with other federal, state, and local agencies to develop common and joint IMAAC emergency response practices, including procedures for dealing with contradictory plume modeling information, to refine the concept of operations for chemical, biological, and radiological releases, and to delineate the type and scale of major CBRN incidents that would qualify for IMAAC assistance; and, in conjunction with IMAAC, work with the federal plume modeling community to accelerate research and development to address plume model deficiencies in urban areas and improve federal modeling and assessment capabilities, including improvements to meteorological information, plume models, and data sets to evaluate plume models.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report does not settle which agency should be responsible for developing, testing, and certifying detection equipment for first responders; it finds no agency currently has that mission for radiological detection equipment in the atmosphere, and DHS's stated mission to test and certify chemical and biological detection equipment is limited to equipment DHS is developing, not equipment first responders buy from manufacturers. The report does not resolve whether commercially available detection equipment performs as manufacturers claim, because DHS does not independently test or verify those claims and the report states it has not independently evaluated what technologies earlier programs evaluated or the SAVER assessments. The report notes that plume models have not been adequately validated and that evaluation and field studies show an unpredictable range of uncertainty, and the Department of Commerce stated that even with implementation of the report's recommendations, plume models would still have limitations as a primary tool for tracking CBRN releases in urban areas. The report also notes open questions about the effects of low-level CBRN exposure on civilian populations, especially vulnerable populations, and states that dose response parameters for the general population do not exist for most chemical warfare agents. It also records DHS's view that GAO should consider alternative scenarios in which first responders are assisted by state and federal agencies with state-of-the-art equipment, and it notes that manufacturers of handheld immunoassays expressed concern about the methods, objectivity, and overall quality of the CDC/FBI evaluation study.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a U.S. Government Accountability Office report (GAO-08-525, issued June 27, 2008) on federal agency efforts to encrypt sensitive information. It addresses three objectives: how commercially available encryption technologies can help federal agencies protect sensitive information and reduce risks; the federal laws, policies, and guidance for using encryption technologies; and the extent to which 24 major federal agencies have implemented or planned to implement encryption. It is based on a survey of 24 agencies, a review of laws, policies, and guidance, and testing of encryption practices at 6 selected agencies.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report's findings, based on GAO's own survey and testing, are that commercially available encryption technologies can help agencies reduce risks, but most agencies had only begun to encrypt sensitive information on mobile computers and devices and none had completed these efforts or documented comprehensive implementation plans. Agencies reported in July through September 2007 that about 70 percent of laptop computers and handheld mobile computing devices combined had not yet been encrypted. Encryption of transmitted information was further along than encryption of stored information: 18 of 23 agencies reported encrypting nearly all or all wired Internet transmissions of sensitive information, and 12 of 21 agencies reported doing so for wireless transmissions. At 6 selected agencies, GAO found that 2 had not installed FIPS-validated cryptographic modules, 4 had not configured installed encryption technologies in accordance with FIPS 140-2, all 6 had not developed or documented policies and procedures for managing encryption implementation, and 3 had not adequately trained personnel. The report concludes that sensitive federal information remains at increased risk of unauthorized disclosure, modification, or loss until these weaknesses are addressed.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The report includes the following figures: in 2006, the Department of Veterans Affairs reported the theft of an unencrypted laptop and external hard drive containing the personal information of approximately 26.5 million veterans and U.S. military personnel. Incidents reported to US-CERT increased from 3,634 in fiscal year 2005 to 5,503 in fiscal year 2006 and 13,029 in fiscal year 2007, about a 259 percent increase. Among 24 major federal agencies, 10 reported systems containing sensitive medical information, 16 reported sensitive regulatory information, 19 reported sensitive personal information, and 20 reported sensitive program-specific information. Of 24 agencies, 8 reported encrypting information on less than 20 percent of their laptop computers and handheld devices, 5 on 20 to 39 percent, 2 on 40 to 59 percent, 3 on 60 to 79 percent, and 6 on 80 to 100 percent; overall, about 70 percent of laptop computers and handheld devices had not been encrypted. Of 22 agencies, 10 reported encrypting less than 20 percent of portable storage media taken offsite and 3 reported encrypting between 20 and 39 percent; of 17 agencies, 9 reported encrypting less than 20 percent of offsite backup storage media. Of 23 agencies reporting on wired Internet transmissions, 18 reported encrypting 80 to 100 percent; of 21 agencies reporting on wireless transmissions, 12 reported encrypting 80 to 100 percent. At the 6 tested agencies, 2 had not installed FIPS-validated cryptographic modules, 4 had not configured installed encryption technologies in accordance with FIPS 140-2, all 6 had not developed or documented policies and procedures, and 3 had not adequately trained personnel. On tested laptop computers, HUD had not installed encryption on any, Education had not installed a FIPS-validated product on any of 15 tested laptops, 3 agencies had installed FIPS-compliant technologies on all 58 tested laptops, and NASA had installed its encryption software on 27 of 29 tested laptops. The report makes 20 recommendations to OMB and six agencies.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report makes 20 recommendations for executive action. It recommends that the Director of the Office of Management and Budget clarify governmentwide policy requiring agencies to encrypt sensitive agency data through additional guidance and/or educational activities, and monitor the effectiveness of agencies' encryption implementation plans and efforts to inventory the sensitive information they hold. It recommends that the Secretary of Agriculture direct the chief information officer to establish and implement a mechanism to monitor the successful installation and effective functioning of encryption products, develop and implement departmentwide procedures for encryption key establishment and management, and develop and implement a training program for technical support and end-user personnel. It recommends that the Secretary of Education direct the chief information officer to evaluate, select, and install FIPS 140-compliant products for all encryption needs and document an implementation plan; configure installed FIPS-compliant encryption technologies in accordance with FIPS-validated cryptographic module security settings; develop and implement departmentwide policy and procedures for encryption key establishment and management; develop and implement departmentwide procedures for use of FIPS-compliant cryptography; and develop and implement a training program. It recommends that the Secretary of Housing and Urban Development direct the chief information officer to evaluate, select, and install FIPS 140-compliant products and document an implementation plan; configure installed FIPS-compliant encryption technologies in accordance with FIPS-validated security settings; and develop and implement departmentwide procedures for FIPS-compliant cryptography and encryption key establishment and management. It recommends that the Secretary of State and the Administrator of the General Services Administration each direct the chief information officer to develop and implement departmentwide policy and procedures for encryption key establishment and management, and develop and implement departmentwide procedures for use of FIPS-compliant cryptography. It recommends that the Administrator of NASA direct the chief information officer to establish and implement a mechanism to monitor the successful installation and effective functioning of encryption products, develop and implement departmentwide policy and procedures for encryption key establishment and management, and develop and implement a training program.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report states that agency uncertainty regarding the applicability of OMB's encryption requirements hampered progress. OMB officials stated in April 2008 that the term 'mobile computers and devices' was intended to include all agency laptops, handheld devices, and portable storage devices, but the report notes this description is not clear in any of OMB's memorandums. The report also notes that none of the 24 agencies had documented comprehensive encryption implementation plans, 18 agencies had not completed inventories of sensitive information, and OMB did not provide evidence that it monitored agencies' efforts to inventory sensitive information or develop implementation plans. It further states that implementing encryption incorrectly, such as failing to properly configure the product, secure encryption keys, or train users, can create a false sense of security and even render data permanently inaccessible.

audience.text: This report is addressed to congressional requesters, specifically the Chairman of the House Committee on Homeland Security, the Chairwoman of its Subcommittee on Intelligence, Information Sharing and Terrorism Risk Assessment, and Representative Zoe Lofgren, to inform their oversight of federal information security.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report, issued June 19, 2008, responds to a directive in the joint explanatory statement accompanying the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2008, to assess the adequacy of the Department of Energy's analysis of pension and medical liabilities. It provides information on (1) DOE's analysis supporting its approval of the April 2006 policy changes in Notice 351.1, (2) DOE's liabilities broken out by contractors' defined benefit pension and postretirement plan components and among its management and operating and other site contracts, and (3) DOE's recent actions to manage its future costs and liabilities. The report transmits briefing slides and includes DOE's written comments and GAO's responses.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: GAO found that DOE officials said the decisions underlying Notice 351.1 were informed over a period of years by trends in cost reimbursements, budgetary uncertainties, and consulting actuaries and others, and that the documentation DOE provided demonstrated it recognized the historical and possible future trend of its liabilities and costs. However, DOE officials acknowledged that there was no formal compiled record or summary analysis of the documentation and factors considered before Notice 351.1 was issued. GAO found only limited evidence that DOE had considered policy alternatives, stakeholder sensitivities, or the near- and long-term financial and mission impacts of the changes, and the decision document reflecting the Deputy Secretary's approval did not include the basis on which approval was recommended. DOE disagreed that the issuance was not based on considered analysis, but GAO disagreed. GAO also reported that, as of September 30, 2007, benefit obligations for DOE contractors' defined benefit pension and postretirement plans were approximately $27.5 billion and $10.5 billion, respectively, with a resulting net funded status of $69.5 million and $10.3 billion. Since 2005, DOE awarded 14 contracts containing new provisions designed to limit pension and postretirement benefits for new employees to no more than 105 percent of comparable organizations, although current policy does not require defined contribution pension plans for new employees. DOE expects these provisions will not substantially affect costs and liabilities for the next 20 to 30 years because they are directed at new employees.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: DOE currently has 43 management and operating and other site contracts that cost over $16 billion annually. In 2007, DOE's financial statements reported that contractors contributed $387 million and $334 million to defined benefit pension and postretirement plans, respectively, and DOE reported a net liability of $69.5 million for defined benefit pensions and $10.3 billion for postretirement benefits. As of September 30, 2007, benefit obligations for DOE contractors' defined benefit pension and postretirement plans were approximately $27.5 billion and $10.5 billion, respectively; assets were $27.4 billion and $161.6 million. The report's table gives benefit obligations of ($27,512.9) million for pension plans and ($10,318.6) million for postretirement plans, assets of $27,443.4 million and $161.6 million, and funded status (net liability) of ($69.5) million and ($10,480.2) million. The net funded status of contractor pension plans changed from an underfunding of $4.5 billion in fiscal year 2006 to an underfunding of $69.5 million in fiscal year 2007. From fiscal years 1997 to 2007, the net funded status of contractor postretirement benefits generally declined from an underfunding of $5.0 billion to an underfunding of $10.3 billion. Figure 1 lists pension funded status for fiscal years 1997-2007 as $4.1 billion, $5.2 billion, $8.2 billion, $10.2 billion, $5.1 billion, -$1.0 billion, -$3.6 billion, -$4.1 billion, -$5.7 billion, -$4.5 billion, and -$0.1 billion. Figure 2 lists postretirement funded status for the same years as -$5.0 billion, -$5.3 billion, -$4.6 billion, -$5.4 billion, -$6.8 billion, -$8.3 billion, -$9.7 billion, -$9.9 billion, -$11.4 billion, -$11.3 billion, and -$10.3 billion. As of September 30, 2007, there were 46 defined benefit pension plans: 12 overfunded and 34 underfunded. Overfunded plans totaled $1,906.8 million and underfunded plans totaled ($1,976.3) million. Eleven of the 12 overfunded plans, sponsored by National Nuclear Security Administration and Office of Science contractors, represent 98 percent of the $1.9 billion in pension overfunding; plans for three facilities represent 56 percent of the total overfunding. Nine of the 34 underfunded plans, sponsored by Office of Environmental Management contractors, represent 61 percent of the $2.0 billion in total pension underfunding; plans for two facilities represent 57 percent of the total underfunding. Employer contributions to all pension plans in fiscal year 2007 were $387.4 million, employee contributions were $3.0 million, and benefit payments were $1,311.5 million. The number of defined benefit pension plan participants as of October 1, 2006, was 77.7 thousand active and 180.0 thousand total. As of September 30, 2007, postretirement plans included health plans for 41 contractors, dental plans for 19, life insurance plans for 23, and Medicare Part B premium reimbursement for 5. The postretirement net liability of $10.3 billion was net of $161.6 million in assets, of which $120.6 million was attributable to a life insurance plan for employees of a single facility. DOE Order 350.1 requires contractors to benchmark their total benefit package against at least 15 comparable organizations, with at most 20 percent of those organizations being DOE contractors; a score exceeding 105 percent of the comparison group's average may lead DOE to require a corrective action plan. Since 2005, DOE awarded 14 contracts containing new pension and postretirement benefit provisions: 2 by NNSA, 6 by Environmental Management, and 6 by the Office of Science. The new contracts direct contractors to perform a benefit value study every 2 years and a cost study annually. GAO reviewed four plan changes: one increased pension obligations by almost $4 million (0.2 percent of plan obligations), one reduced retiree health obligations by $105.8 million (7.8 percent), and two reduced retiree life insurance obligations by a total of $112.3 million (5.5 percent).

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: Not stated in this document.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report states that GAO limited its review to DOE's policies for reimbursing allowable contractor benefit costs and did not audit or verify data provided by DOE or its contractors for individual benefit plan activity and balances, although the data were determined to be consistent in the aggregate with DOE's financial statements and sufficiently reliable for the purposes of the review. GAO also did not audit or verify the amount or timing of payments by DOE to its contractors for allowable benefit costs or any other costs. The limited number of plan changes reviewed did not provide a basis for a conclusion on DOE's internal controls over benefit plan changes. The review of DOE's actions to manage future costs and liabilities did not include identifying all actions DOE may have taken or evaluating the nature, extent, or effect of any such actions. GAO neither verified the accuracy of the results of benefit value studies nor evaluated contractors' conformance with DOE's requirements and guidance for performing such studies. Because DOE believes funded status amounts and benefit value scores may be proprietary, information that could associate a funded status amount or benefit value score with a particular facility or contractor was removed from the report. GAO also stated that the connection between what DOE cites as evidence of its concerns and its policy changes as reflected in Notice 351.1 is not readily apparent from the documents DOE provided, and that DOE's materials did not include a comprehensive assessment of existing DOE policies, an analysis of the potential impacts of alternative strategies, or an indication of the information that senior DOE management relied on.

audience.text: The report is addressed to the Chairmen and Ranking Members of the Subcommittee on Energy and Water Development of the Senate and House Committees on Appropriations, and it supports congressional oversight and appropriation decisions regarding DOE's management of contractor pension and postretirement benefit costs and liabilities.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a U.S. Government Accountability Office report, GAO-08-645, issued June 23, 2008, titled 'Electronic Payments: Many Programs Electronically Disburse Federal Benefits, and More Outreach Could Increase Use.' It examines the extent to which federal benefit programs use electronic payment methods to disburse benefits, the factors agencies consider when implementing or using electronic payments, and options for increasing electronic payment use, particularly actions by the Department of the Treasury. The scope includes a survey of 42 federal benefit programs, interviews with six federal agencies, state and tribal agencies, industry and consumer groups, and a site visit to Harrisburg, Pennsylvania.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: Most federal benefit programs surveyed (34 of 42) used one or more electronic payment methods, and direct deposit was the most common method; 6 programs did not use electronic payments and 2 were unsure. Data limitations prevented determining the extent of electronic payment use for most programs; 18 of 42 programs provided data, and among those the percentage of payments made electronically ranged from about 5 to 100 percent, while for the 5 largest of these programs by dollar value, about 54 to 100 percent of payments were made electronically. Eight of those 18 programs paid 100 percent of benefit payments electronically, but 6 of the 8 were education assistance programs that typically paid institutions rather than individuals. Of the 13 programs that provided paper-check data, 9 distributed less than half of the total dollar value of benefit payments by paper check and 4 distributed 100 percent by paper check. Agencies consider financial burden to recipients, program and recipient characteristics, program costs, and fraud and security risks when deciding whether to use electronic payments. Options for increasing use include new statutory requirements, public outreach, adapting payment cards, making electronic payment the default, and Treasury initiatives such as Go Direct and Direct Express. The report recommends regular Treasury outreach to federal agencies.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: Among the survey numbers: 34 of 42 programs (81 percent) used electronic payments; 6 did not; 2 were unsure. Of the 34, 25 used direct deposit, 9 used EBT, and 8 used another type of EPC; 16 were needs-based; 20 were administered at the federal level; about half paid cash benefits monthly. 18 of 42 programs provided data on the percentage of payments made electronically, ranging from about 5 to 100 percent; for the 5 largest of these, about 54 to 100 percent. 8 of the 18 paid 100 percent electronically, 6 of which were education assistance programs. 13 of 42 provided paper-check data; 9 distributed less than half of total dollar value by paper check; 4 distributed 100 percent by paper check. 20 of 34 (about 59 percent) said all, almost all, or most recipients received electronic payments; 23 of 34 (68 percent) said about half or more. The 6 programs not using electronic payments each had fewer than 3 million recipients and expended less than $500 million in fiscal year 2006; 4 had fewer than 100,000 recipients; the WIC Farmers' Market Nutrition Program had about 2.5 million recipients; Survivors and Dependents Educational Assistance expended about $495 million. Social Security Retirement Insurance distributed $418,056,535,776 in fiscal year 2006 and had 33,945,000 recipients; Food Stamp had 26,671,819 recipients. 7 of the 34 electronic-payment programs paid less than $20 million in fiscal year 2006, 15 paid $100 million to $10 billion, and the rest more than $10 billion. The survey identified 455 programs, selected 45, and analyzed 42; the response rate was 100 percent. Treasury's FMS annually disburses almost 1 billion payments with a dollar value of more than $1.6 trillion. As of fiscal year 2008 through January, about 88 percent of all Treasury-disbursed payments are benefit payments. Treasury's electronic benefit payment share was 56 percent in fiscal year 1996, 62 percent in fiscal year 1997, 68 percent in fiscal year 1998, 73 percent in fiscal year 1999, 75 percent in fiscal year 2000, 76 percent in fiscal year 2001, 77 percent in fiscal year 2002, 77 percent in fiscal year 2003, 78 percent in fiscal year 2004, 79 percent in fiscal year 2005, 80 percent in fiscal year 2006, 81 percent in fiscal year 2007, and 81.6 percent in fiscal year 2008 through January. There were about 90,000 active Electronic Transfer Accounts at the time of the review. Over the last 3 years, 1.8 million recipients converted from paper checks to direct deposit. In the Direct Express pilot, about 3,000 unbanked Social Security and SSI recipients in Illinois participated; 85 percent of card users were satisfied and 88 percent would refer the program. Direct Express was piloted in January 2007 and launched nationwide in April 2008. In 2006, the number of electronic payments was 62.7 billion with a value of $34.1 trillion, compared with 30.6 billion checks paid with a value of $41.7 trillion. The average annual rate of decline in checks paid was estimated at 3.3 percent between 1995 and 2000 and 4.3 percent between 2000 and 2003. By 2003, electronic payments exceeded check payments for the first time.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Secretary of the Treasury direct Treasury's Commissioner of the Financial Management Service to consider developing a process for conducting outreach to federal agencies on a more regular basis, with the goal of identifying opportunities for increasing the use of electronic payments. For example, Treasury could meet with agency CFOs or their designees and with staff from smaller agencies, on a semiannual or annual basis, to discuss challenges agencies face in moving to electronic payments and identify actions Treasury and agencies could take to facilitate the transition. Treasury generally agreed with the report, did not comment on the recommendation, and stated that it would address the recommendation in its statement of actions to congressional committees not later than 60 days after the report date. USDA officials stated that they agreed with the overall message of the report.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report does not settle the extent of electronic payment use for most federal benefit programs: data limitations prevented GAO from determining the percentage of payments made electronically for 24 of the 42 surveyed programs, in part because states disburse payments for many programs and are not required to provide specific payment data to the overseeing federal agency. The report states that its final selection of programs was a nonrandom, nongeneralizable sample. It notes that CFDA and FAADS data are self-reported by agencies and may have missing or incorrect information, and that not all survey questions were answered, particularly the questions on the total dollar value of benefits paid electronically and by paper check. It also notes that consumer and special interest groups have not supported a mandatory electronic delivery method, and that Treasury had no plans to conduct outreach to CFO agencies and smaller agencies on a regular basis. Treasury did not comment on the recommendation.

audience.text: This report is addressed to the Ranking Member, Committee on Oversight and Government Reform, House of Representatives, and supports congressional oversight, policy, and funding decisions.
