about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This is a June 2008 U.S. Government Accountability Office report to congressional requesters about young adults aged 18 through 26 with serious mental illness. It provides information on the number and demographic characteristics of these young adults, the challenges they face, how selected states (Connecticut, Maryland, Massachusetts, and Mississippi) assist them, and how the federal government supports states and coordinates federal programs that can assist them.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: Based on its own analysis of survey and administrative data and site visits to four states, GAO finds that at least 2.4 million young adults aged 18 through 26, or 6.5 percent of the estimated 37 million young adults in U.S. households, had a serious mental illness in 2006, and that estimate is likely low because the underlying survey excluded homeless, institutionalized, and incarcerated individuals. Most (89 percent) had more than one diagnosed disorder, and 32 percent also had alcohol or drug abuse or dependence. Young adults with serious mental illness had lower high school graduation rates (64 percent versus 83 percent for those with no mental illness) and lower postsecondary education rates (32 percent versus 51 percent). About 186,000 young adults received SSI or DI benefits in 2006 because their mental illness was severe enough to prevent substantial gainful activity. The report also finds that young adults with serious mental illness face challenges finding age-appropriate services, qualifying for adult programs, and navigating multiple programs and delivery systems. The four states visited have developed programs offering multidimensional, age-appropriate services, but none of the programs have been systematically evaluated. Federal agencies have supported demonstrations, technical assistance, and research and have formed interagency working groups, but no federal programs specifically target this population.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The report's figures include: at least 2.4 million young adults aged 18 through 26, or 6.5 percent of the 37 million non-institutionalized young adults in that age range, had a serious mental illness in 2006; another 9.3 million, or 25.3 percent, had a moderate or mild mental illness; 68.2 percent had no mental illness; 89 percent had two or more diagnoses and 56 percent had four or more; 32 percent had a co-occurring alcohol or drug abuse or dependence diagnosis. Among those with serious mental illness, 45 percent had intermittent explosive disorder, 32 percent major depressive disorder, 32 percent specific phobia, 28 percent bipolar disorder, 28 percent social phobia, and 26 percent alcohol abuse; 20 percent of those with intermittent explosive disorder also had bipolar disorder and 39 percent also had alcohol abuse. Education rates were 64 percent high school graduation and 32 percent postsecondary education for those with serious mental illness, versus 83 percent and 51 percent for those with no mental illness; employment rates were 63 percent versus 68 percent for those with mild or moderate mental illness and 71 percent for those with no mental illness. A 1994-95 survey found a 34 percent employment rate among working-age adults with mental health disabilities versus 79 percent among adults with no disability, and the President's New Freedom Commission stated in 2003 that only one in three persons with a disability resulting from mental illness is employed. About 186,000 young adults received SSI or DI in 2006, just under a quarter of all young adults receiving SSI or DI that year; 67 percent received SSI only, 9 percent received DI only, 24 percent received concurrent payments, and nearly 60 percent of those receiving SSI first became eligible before age 18. Among these beneficiaries, 46 percent had affective mood disorders, 33 percent had schizophrenic or other functional psychotic disorders, 8 percent had anxiety disorders, 5 percent had personality disorders, and 8 percent had other mental disorders. SSI and DI recipients had a 52 percent high school graduation rate versus 64 percent for all young adults with serious mental illness, a 15 percent current employment rate versus 63 percent, and average annual household income of $20,685 versus $45,667 according to the 2004 National Beneficiary Survey and the 2001-2003 NCS-R; 59 percent had ever worked. Another 100,000 young adults had a secondary diagnosis of mental illness and were not included in the 186,000 count. In foster care research, a national survey of 464 individuals aged 12 to 17 placed in foster care found they were about four times more likely to have attempted suicide and three times more likely to have experienced significant anxiety and mood symptoms; the Northwest Foster Care Alumni Study of 659 adults aged 20 through 33 found over half had symptoms of one or more mental disorders in the previous year, 20 percent had symptoms of three or more, versus 3 percent in the NCS-R. An Urban Institute study found 46 percent of homeless individuals aged 20 through 24 had experienced a mental health problem in the prior year; a Los Angeles study of 432 homeless young people found 63 percent of those aged 19 through 24 had depressive symptoms and 38 percent had attempted suicide. Bureau of Justice Statistics surveys found 62.6 percent of young adults aged 24 or younger in state prisons had a mental health problem in 2004 and 70.3 percent of those in local jails in 2002; a multi-state juvenile justice survey found 70 percent of youth involved with the juvenile justice system had at least one mental health disorder and 27 percent had a severe disorder. Program figures include $126.4 billion in SSI and DI benefits paid in fiscal year 2006, $317 billion in Medicaid spending in 2006, nearly $43 million in Medicaid Infrastructure Grants available in fiscal year 2008, nearly $14 million in Real Choice Systems Change Grants awarded in fiscal year 2007, $401 million in SAMHSA block grants in fiscal year 2007, which averaged 1 to 2 percent of each state's community-based mental health budget, approximately $940 million appropriated for WIA youth activities in 2006, over $2.8 billion appropriated for vocational rehabilitation in 2007, $140 million in Chafee Foster Care Independence program funding in 2006, and up to $5,000 per year in Chafee Education and Training Vouchers. The Bazelon Center identified 57 relevant federal programs in 2005. Connecticut's specialized young adult program served 716 individuals in state fiscal year 2007, about 27 percent of the 2,615 young adults with serious mental illness receiving services from the state mental health agency; Massachusetts served all approximately 2,600 young adults aged 16 to 25 with serious mental illness in its mental health system in 2007; Maryland approved 30 supported employment programs; Mississippi's Multidisciplinary Assessment and Planning Teams operated in 33 of 82 counties; HUD reported the median age of heads of households receiving HUD supportive housing was 47; and one service provider in Massachusetts was using 10 Section 8 vouchers to serve 20 to 30 young adults. SSA officials said 25 percent of youth who received SSI because of a mental health-related condition do not qualify for SSI once they turn 18.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document makes no recommendations. It describes steps that some states and federal agencies are already taking, but it does not call for any specific action.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that its prevalence estimate of 2.4 million young adults is likely low because the NCS-R excluded individuals who were institutionalized, incarcerated, or homeless, did not measure schizophrenia and other nonaffective psychotic disorders, and may underreport socially unacceptable behaviors. It was unable to identify the number of young adults with serious mental illness who were homeless or involved in the justice or foster care systems, and it says no studies produced national estimates for those groups with consistent measures. It also states that the 186,000 SSI and DI count could be higher because some individuals do not apply or complete the application process and because about 100,000 young adults with a secondary diagnosis of mental illness were not included. The report notes that the evidence-based practices used by states have not been empirically tested specifically on the young adult population, and that none of the four state programs have been systematically evaluated for effectiveness. It also notes that HHS expressed confusion over the definition of serious mental illness and said the report's scope could be expanded in a number of ways.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) report, GAO-08-723, issued August 2008, on the Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) and the federal Health Center Program. The report examines (1) for 2006, the extent to which federally designated medically underserved areas (MUAs) lacked health center sites and the services provided by each site in an MUA; (2) how new access point grants awarded in 2007 changed the extent to which MUAs lacked health center sites; and (3) HRSA's oversight of cooperative agreement recipients' assistance to new access point applicants and the feedback HRSA provides to unsuccessful applicants.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: These findings are the report's own, based on GAO's analysis of HRSA and U.S. Census Bureau data. GAO found that in 2006, 47 percent of MUAs nationwide—1,600 of 3,421—lacked a health center site, with wide variation by census region and state; for example, 62 percent of MUAs in the Midwest lacked a site versus 32 percent in the West, and more than 80 percent lacked a site in Nebraska and Iowa while fewer than 25 percent lacked one in Mississippi and California. GAO could not determine the types of services provided at individual sites because HRSA does not collect and maintain readily available site-level data, so the extent to which MUA residents have access to the full range of comprehensive primary care services is unknown. GAO found that HRSA's 2007 new access point awards reduced the number of MUAs lacking a site by about 7 percent, from 1,600 to 1,487, leaving 43 percent of MUAs without a site in 2007, and that wide geographic variation remained. GAO also found that HRSA's oversight of training and technical assistance cooperative agreement recipients is limited because the agency lacks standardized performance measures and is unlikely to meet its policy of comprehensive on-site reviews every 3 to 5 years, and that 38 percent of summary statements sent to unsuccessful applicants contained unclear feedback.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The report states that in 2006 Health Center Program grants made up about 20 percent of all health center grantees' revenues, and approximately 1,000 health center grantees operated more than 6,000 health center sites while serving more than 15 million people. For fiscal year 2007, HRSA awarded nearly $53 million in cooperative agreements to national organizations and regional and state primary care associations. In 2006, 47 percent of MUAs nationwide—1,600 of 3,421—lacked a health center site; the Midwest had the most (62 percent) and the West the fewest (32 percent). More than three-quarters of MUAs lacked a site in Nebraska (91 percent), Iowa (82 percent), Minnesota (77 percent), and Montana (77 percent), while fewer than one-quarter lacked a site in Colorado (21 percent), California (20 percent), Mississippi (20 percent), and West Virginia (19 percent). In 2006, 32 percent of all MUAs contained more than one health center site, and among MUAs with at least one site, 60 percent contained multiple sites. The 2007 new access point awards reduced the number of MUAs lacking a site by about 7 percent: 113 fewer MUAs, from 1,600 in 2006 to 1,487 in 2007, leaving 43 percent of MUAs lacking a site in 2007. By census region, the percentage of MUAs lacking a site changed from 2006 to 2007 as follows: Northeast, 39 to 37; South, 45 to 40; Midwest, 62 to 60; and West, 32 to 31. The number and percentage decrease by region were: Northeast, 153 to 147, a decrease of 6 (4 percent); Midwest, 641 to 617, a decrease of 24 (4 percent); South, 651 to 574, a decrease of 77 (12 percent); West, 155 to 149, a decrease of 6 (4 percent); nationally, 1,600 to 1,487, a decrease of 113 (7 percent). In 2007, 202 new access point grants were awarded: 39 (19 percent) in the Midwest, 15 (7 percent) in the Northeast, 101 (50 percent) in the South, and 47 (23 percent) in the West. In the High Poverty County competition, 69 percent of awards went to applicants from the South, and nearly two-thirds of the 200 targeted counties were in the South. In the 2007 open new access point competition, 127 grants were awarded: 21 (17 percent) in the Midwest, 12 (9 percent) in the Northeast, 49 (39 percent) in the South, and 45 (35 percent) in the West. HRSA has conducted comprehensive on-site reviews for fewer than one-quarter—about 20 percent—of its training and technical assistance cooperative agreement recipients targeting new access point applicants since the reviews were implemented in 2004. Of 69 summary statements sampled from the 230 sent to unsuccessful applicants in fiscal years 2005 and 2007, 38 percent contained unclear feedback, 13 percent contained unclear feedback in more than one criterion, and GAO found 41 distinct examples of unclear feedback.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: GAO recommends that the Administrator of HRSA take four actions to improve the Health Center Program: collect and maintain readily available data on the types of services provided at each health center site to improve the agency's ability to measure access to comprehensive primary care services in MUAs; develop and implement standardized performance measures for training and technical assistance cooperative agreement recipients that assist applicants, including a measure of the number of successful applicants a recipient assisted; reevaluate the policy of requiring comprehensive on-site reviews of training and technical assistance cooperative agreement recipients every 3 to 5 years and consider targeting available resources to cooperative agreement recipients most likely to benefit from such oversight; and identify and take appropriate action to ensure that the discussion of an applicant's strengths and weaknesses in all summary statements is clear.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report states that it could not determine the types of primary care services provided at each health center site because HRSA does not collect and maintain readily available site-level data, leaving unknown the extent to which individuals in MUAs have access to the full range of comprehensive primary care services. It also states that because HRSA lacks this information, HRSA's ability to assess the full range of services in needy areas when considering the placement of new access points and to evaluate service area overlap in MUAs is limited. The report notes methodological caveats: because zip-code-level analysis was used, an MUA's boundary in the analysis may be larger than HRSA's definition, so the analysis may overestimate the number of MUAs that contain a health center site; and because the 2007 UDS data were not yet updated, GAO assumed all 2006 health center sites were still operating in 2007. The report also states that GAO did not examine whether MUAs were sufficiently served because that was beyond the scope of the work. HHS raised concerns not resolved by the report: that the report excluded medically underserved populations (MUPs) and did not account for health center sites located near but outside MUA boundaries; that the percentage-of-MUAs-lacking-a-site indicator may be of limited utility because MUAs differ in size, geographic location, and demographic characteristics; that the analysis presumed one site could be sufficient to serve an MUA; that a health center site may not be the appropriate solution for some small-population MUAs; and that collecting site-specific service data would burden grantees and raise administrative expenses. The report also notes that HRSA officials said they are developing standardized performance measures but provided no details, so it is unclear to what extent the proposed measures will allow HRSA to assess the performance of cooperative agreement recipients.

audience.text: The report is addressed to the Ranking Member of the Subcommittee on Oversight and Investigations, Committee on Energy and Commerce, House of Representatives, for congressional oversight of HRSA's Health Center Program.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This is a U.S. Government Accountability Office report (GAO-08-741) issued June 2008 to the Ranking Member of the Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity, House Committee on Veterans' Affairs. It examines whether veteran students receive less federal financial aid than nonveterans by determining (1) how the amount of Title IV financial aid awarded to veteran students compares with that awarded to nonveteran students, (2) how higher education institutions allocate Title IV financial aid among veteran and nonveteran students, and (3) how federal agencies and higher education institutions provide information to veterans on Title IV financial aid. The scope covers veterans and active-duty personnel who served for 3 or more years and received Chapter 30 GI benefits, compared with nonveteran independent students, using academic year 2005 to 2006 data for Pell Grants and Stafford Loans, academic year 2003 to 2004 data for campus-based aid, and academic year 2005 to 2006 Chapter 30 GI benefit rates; reservists are excluded from the scope.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report finds that, overall, veteran students received similar amounts of Title IV aid as nonveteran, independent students, but when Chapter 30 GI benefits were included, veterans received more total federal aid than nonveterans. Veterans received, on average, 6 percent less in Pell Grants than nonveterans in academic year 2005 to 2006, and the report attributes this to veterans tending to have higher incomes rather than to receipt of Chapter 30 GI benefits, which are not counted as income for Pell Grant eligibility. Veterans received similar amounts of subsidized and unsubsidized Stafford Loans as nonveterans in academic year 2005 to 2006, and similar amounts of campus-based aid in academic year 2003 to 2004, with the campus-based aid numbers not significantly different at the 95 percent confidence level. The report also finds that laws and regulations largely dictate how schools allocate Title IV aid among veteran and nonveteran students, but five of the eight schools interviewed used their limited flexibility to allow veterans to be eligible for larger amounts of certain types of Title IV aid. Federal agencies and schools provide the same information on Title IV aid to all students, two of the eight schools reached out to veteran students at nearby military bases, and the Department of Education in 2007 began efforts such as workshops on federal aid for personnel separating from the military; the Department of Veterans Affairs does not provide Title IV information directly to students but refers them to school financial aid offices.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The document reports the following figures. Over the past decade, average college tuition and fees increased between 20 and 38 percent, depending on the type of institution. In fiscal year 2007, the Department of Education provided $82 billion in Title IV financial aid to 11 million students and their families. In fiscal year 2007, the Department of Veterans Affairs awarded about $2 billion in Chapter 30 education benefits under the Montgomery GI Bill to more than 300,000 veteran students. For first-year undergraduates, annual Pell Grant awards were $400 to $4,050 in award year 2005 to 2006 and $400 to $4,310 in award year 2007 to 2008; subsidized Stafford Loans were up to $2,625 in academic year 2005 to 2006 and up to $3,500 in academic year 2007 to 2008; unsubsidized Stafford Loans were up to $6,625 for independent undergraduates, including any subsidized loan amounts received for the same period, in academic year 2005 to 2006 and up to $7,500 in academic year 2007 to 2008. Federal Supplemental Educational Opportunity Grants were $100 to $4,000, except up to $4,400 for a study-abroad program, in award years 2005 to 2006 and 2007 to 2008; Federal Perkins Loans were up to $4,000 in award years 2005 to 2006 and 2007 to 2008; Federal Work-Study had no annual minimum or maximum award amounts up to the student's financial need in award years 2005 to 2006 and 2007 to 2008. For Chapter 30 GI benefits, servicemembers must contribute $100 per month for the first 12 months of service, and in academic year 2005 to 2006, individuals who completed 3 or more years of active duty and attended a college or university full-time received $1,034 per month for a maximum of 36 months. Average aid amounts for first-year full-time students were: Pell Grant $2,322 for veterans and $2,482 for nonveteran independent students in 2005 to 2006; subsidized Stafford Loan $2,082 for veterans and $2,109 for nonveteran independent students in 2005 to 2006; unsubsidized Stafford Loan $2,959 for veterans and $2,945 for nonveteran independent students in 2005 to 2006; campus-based aid $1,450, an estimate, for veterans and $1,300, an estimate, for nonveteran independent students in 2003 to 2004, with these numbers not significantly different at the 95 percent confidence level; and Chapter 30 GI benefits $9,306 for veterans and N/A for nonveteran independent students in 2005 to 2006. Veterans received, on average, 6 percent less in Pell Grants than nonveterans in academic year 2005 to 2006. In the report's example for public 2-year schools at the 75th income percentile, veterans earned an average of $38,550 in the year before starting school compared with $33,259 for nonveterans, and veterans were eligible for a Pell Grant of $1,600 compared with $2,100 for nonveterans. Appendix III also reports estimated aid for first-year students at public 2-year institutions with an average cost of attendance of $11,692, public 4-year institutions with $15,566, private not-for-profit 4-year institutions with $31,916, and proprietary institutions with $22,931, by income percentile and student classification. Among dependent students who attended proprietary institutions in academic year 2003 to 2004, 20.3 percent received PLUS loans.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document makes no formal recommendations. Its only suggestion of further work appears in the concluding observations, where it states that the report does not address how the federal financial aid amounts reservists receive compare with other students and that this may warrant further inquiry given the increasing number of reservists who have been called to active duty in recent years and important differences in their receipt of GI benefits.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states several limits and open questions. It does not address how the federal financial aid amounts reservists receive compare with other students, because reservists were outside the scope. The eight schools interviewed were a nonprobability sample selected for diversity, so the report states the findings cannot be generalized beyond those schools. The most recent data differed by aid type: academic year 2005 to 2006 for Pell Grants and Stafford Loans, and academic year 2003 to 2004 for campus-based aid. The report notes that the average aid amounts reported may not reflect the total aid received by any individual student, and that individual veterans may be eligible for more Title IV aid but received, on average, similar amounts as nonveterans, with contributing factors possibly including income and students' decisions not to take loans for which they were eligible. The campus-based aid numbers were not significantly different at the 95 percent confidence level. The report also notes that data for students attending private 2-year schools were excluded due to lack of reliable data, and that opinions differ on whether veterans should have advantages in Title IV aid eligibility, such as Chapter 30 GI benefits not being counted as income or as a resource in certain calculations.

audience.name: Who it is for
audience.text: The report is addressed to the Ranking Member of the Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity, Committee on Veterans' Affairs, House of Representatives, and supports congressional oversight of whether veteran students receive less federal financial aid than nonveterans.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a GAO report to congressional committees, issued September 2008, on DOD's implementation of the National Security Personnel System (NSPS). It assesses the extent to which DOD incorporated internal safeguards and accountability mechanisms for the fairness, effectiveness, and credibility of the NSPS performance management system, and it assesses civilian employees' perceptions of NSPS and DOD's actions to address those perceptions.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: GAO found that DOD had taken some steps to implement each of nine internal safeguards, but implementation of three safeguards could be improved immediately: predecisional internal safeguards, reasonable transparency, and meaningful distinctions in employee performance. DOD cannot determine whether NSPS rating results are nondiscriminatory before they are finalized because it does not require a third party to analyze predecisional rating results for anomalies; employees at some installations lack transparency because DOD does not require commands to publish rating distributions, and three of the sites visited decided not to publish them; and NSPS guidance may discourage meaningful distinctions because it emphasized that most employees should be evaluated as a '3' (valued performer), creating hesitancy to award other ratings. GAO also found that NSPS employees were more positive than other DOD employees about some performance-management goals, but employees with the most NSPS experience showed downward movement in attitudes, and discussion groups revealed consistent concerns about morale, time burden, writing skills, pay pool transparency, and pace of implementation. DOD did not have a specific action plan to address the generally negative employee perceptions.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: Over 182,000 DOD civilian employees had been phased into NSPS as of May 2008, with approximately 273,000 remaining; the Fiscal Year 2008 act prohibited conversion of more than 100,000 employees in any calendar year. DOD received over 58,000 comments during rule design, held about 100 focus groups in 2004, used 95 employees in contractor workshops, and received valid survey responses from approximately 14 percent, or 71,000 employees, on work behaviors. Training included 10 hours for employees, 18 hours basic and 24 hours pay pool panel training for managers and supervisors, and 26 or more hours for human resource practitioners. The November 2005 cost estimate was $158 million; a revised estimate put implementation costs at approximately $143 million from fiscal years 2009 through 2011. In the May 2007 Status of Forces Survey, an estimated 43 percent of NSPS employees, compared with 25 percent of all other DOD employees, said pay raises depend on how well employees perform their jobs; an estimated 56 percent of NSPS employees said bonus and cash awards are based on performance compared with 52 percent of all DOD employees, and 40 percent of NSPS supervisors said they could influence pay compared with 27 percent of all DOD supervisors. Among spiral 1.1 employees, agreement that the performance appraisal was a fair reflection of performance declined from an estimated 67 percent in May 2006 to 52 percent in May 2007; agreement that NSPS would have a positive effect on DOD's personnel practices dropped from 40 percent in May 2006 to 23 percent in May 2007; and the estimated percentage saying NSPS was worse than previous systems rose from 44 percent in November 2006 to 50 percent in May 2007. DOD-wide rating distributions were 0.2 percent at level 1, 1.6 percent at level 2, 57.0 percent at level 3, 36.1 percent at level 4, and 5.1 percent at level 5; in the pay pools GAO reviewed, 60 percent or more of employees were rated at level 3 in 9 pay pools. Supervisors said it took a minimum of 4 uninterrupted hours per employee to complete a rating, and employees at 11 of 12 locations raised concerns about writing skills influencing ratings.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document recommends that DOD: require a third party to perform predecisional demographic and other analysis as appropriate for pay pools; require overall final rating results to be published; encourage pay pools and supervisors to use all categories of ratings as appropriate; and develop and implement a specific action plan to address employee perceptions of NSPS ascertained from DOD's surveys and employee focus groups, including actions to mitigate concerns such as the influence of writing skills on pay pool panels' assessments. It also records DOD's responses: DOD concurred with publishing final rating results, partially concurred with using all rating categories and with the action plan, and did not concur with the predecisional analysis recommendation.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that the information from GAO's discussion groups is not generalizable to the entire population of DOD civilians, though it provides insight; GAO was unable to determine whether final rating distributions were meaningful because it lacked specific knowledge of employees' performance within pay pools; and GAO could not identify an overall trend or whether the negative movement in employee attitudes would continue because responses were fairly evenly distributed and more survey administrations are needed. DOD had not developed a new timeline for phasing in the remaining approximately 273,000 employees after legislative changes, and DOD's survey methodology, while generally consistent with standard research practices, had some areas that could be improved. Future implementation costs may accrue if additional employees are later converted to NSPS.

audience.name: Who it is for
audience.text: This document is addressed to the congressional committees specified in the report; it supports congressional oversight of DOD's implementation of NSPS, including the Senate Armed Services Committee request and the Fiscal Year 2008 National Defense Authorization Act mandate.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report, issued September 18, 2008, examines the roles and readiness of five major national voluntary organizations — the American Red Cross, The Salvation Army, the Southern Baptist Convention, Catholic Charities USA, and United Way of America — to provide mass care and other human services in large-scale disasters requiring federal assistance. It reviews federal disaster planning documents, including the 2008 National Response Framework, the Catastrophic Incident Supplement, and Emergency Support Function 6; assesses steps the organizations have taken since Hurricanes Katrina and Rita; reviews what is known about their current sheltering and feeding capabilities in four high-risk metropolitan areas; and identifies remaining challenges. It makes recommendations to FEMA.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The document's findings are that the voluntary organizations reviewed are a major source of mass care and other services in large-scale disasters, with four providing direct services and the United Way mostly conducting fund-raising. The 2008 National Response Framework changed the American Red Cross from the primary agency for mass care to a support agency under ESF-6, because the Red Cross, as a nongovernmental entity, cannot direct federal resources. The Catastrophic Incident Supplement still describes the Red Cross as the primary agency for mass care, has not been updated, and no interim agreement documents the mutual understanding of the Red Cross's support role in a catastrophic event. Since Katrina, the Red Cross has reorganized its chapters and developed community partnerships, and the direct service providers have increased collaboration on feeding, case management, logistics, and communications. Existing assessments of mass care capabilities are incomplete: FEMA's 2007 survey addresses sheltering but not feeding outside shelters and does not include all voluntary organization capabilities, and most organizations have not assessed their own nationwide capabilities. Without government and other assistance, a worst-case large-scale disaster would likely overwhelm the current sheltering and feeding capabilities of voluntary organizations in the four metropolitan areas visited. Remaining challenges include shortages of trained personnel, difficulty dedicating staff and financial resources to preparedness, limited access to DHS preparedness grants, and varying coordination with government agencies; it is too soon to tell how recent Red Cross staffing cuts will affect coordination and service delivery.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The document reports the following figures. Following the 2005 hurricanes, the Red Cross raised more than $2.1 billion; The Salvation Army, $325 million; Catholic Charities USA, $150 million; the United Way, $28 million; and the Southern Baptist Convention, about $20 million. In the Gulf Coast hurricane response, the Red Cross provided more than 52.6 million meals and snacks, opened more than 1,300 shelters across 27 states, provided 3.4 million overnight stays, and used 245,000 volunteers; The Salvation Army provided 7.7 million meals and snacks, 91,400 lodging spaces, 506,443 volunteer hours, and raised $365 million; the Southern Baptist Convention provided more than 14.6 million meals, 165,748 volunteer days, and raised $20 million; Catholic Charities USA provided 51 million pounds of food, had more than 110 dioceses respond, and raised $150 million; and United Way of America raised $28 million. The Red Cross reported about 1,600 national headquarters and service area staff as of May 2008, more than 71,000 nationally deployable volunteers, 733 local chapters, 50,000 potential shelter facilities, and sheltering supplies for up to 500,000 people. It maintains mutual aid agreements with The Salvation Army, the Southern Baptist Convention, Catholic Charities USA, and 39 other organizations under ESF-6. As of June 2007, 2-1-1 coverage served approximately 198 million Americans, about 65 percent of the U.S. population. The Red Cross reported a projected fiscal year 2008 operating budget deficit of about $150 million, reduced staff by about 1,000 in early 2008, eliminated full-time staff at FEMA's 10 regional offices, reduced staff supporting state emergency management agencies from 14 to 5, and requested $7 million annually for ESF-6 staffing plus $3 million for integrating nongovernmental mass care services, for a total of $10 million. During Katrina, approximately 770,000 people were displaced. In the four metropolitan areas, the Red Cross had 386 shelter facilities in Washington, D.C.; 623 in New York; 341 in Los Angeles; and 65 in Miami. DHS estimated a major earthquake in a metropolitan area could necessitate shelter for as many as 300,000 people, and a DHS Target Capabilities List estimate for a 7.2-magnitude earthquake followed by an 8.0 earthquake in a metropolitan area of about 10 million people projected 313,000 people needing shelter and 1.5 million meals per day. The Red Cross's July 2007 Risk-Based Capacity Building Initiative projected 564,113 people needing shelter and 2.5 million people needing feeding in Southern California; 300,000 people needing shelter in the Washington, D.C., region; 605,000 people needing shelter and 4 million people needing feeding in the New York City metro area; and 328,646 people needing shelter and 657,292 meals per day in the Gulf Coast. Florida's Hurricane Ono planning project projected 885,000 people needing shelter and 3 million meals per day in South Florida. Red Cross officials in Los Angeles said their local sheltering capacity was 84,000 people under optimal conditions. The Catastrophic Incident Supplement expects the Red Cross, within 2 hours after implementation, to inventory shelter space in a 250-mile radius of the disaster.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document recommends that the Secretary of Homeland Security direct the Administrator of FEMA to establish a time frame for updating the mass care section of the Catastrophic Incident Supplement so that it is consistent with the ESF-6 changes under the new National Response Framework and no longer requires the Red Cross to direct federal government resources; in the meantime, FEMA should develop an interim agreement with the Red Cross documenting their understanding of the Red Cross's role and responsibilities in a catastrophic event. It also recommends that FEMA take steps to better incorporate voluntary organizations' capabilities into assessments of mass care capabilities, such as FEMA's GAP Analysis, and broaden the assessment to include feeding capabilities outside shelters, including by soliciting input from voluntary organizations such as through NVOAD, integrating voluntary organization data into FEMA's analyses, and encouraging state governments to include voluntary mass care organization data in studies. It further recommends that FEMA clarify the Homeland Security Grant Program funding guidance for states so it is clear that voluntary organizations and local VOADs are among those eligible to be subgrantees under the program. The document notes that FEMA agreed with the recommendations on establishing a time frame for updating the Supplement and clarifying grant guidance, but disagreed with the recommendation on incorporating voluntary organizations' capabilities into assessments.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that it does not attempt to assess the total disaster response capabilities in any single location visited or the efficacy of responses to particular scenarios, such as major earthquakes versus hurricanes. It says estimates of the magnitude of mass care needs in worst-case large-scale disasters are necessarily characterized by uncertainties. It states that initial assessments have not fully captured the collective capabilities of major voluntary organizations, most existing assessments are locally or regionally based, and the field lacks standard terms and measures for characterizing resources. about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This is a U.S. Government Accountability Office report, GAO-08-825, issued September 9, 2008, to congressional requesters, on critical infrastructure protection and the Department of Homeland Security's first Cyber Storm exercise. The report identifies the eight lessons DHS learned from Cyber Storm I, assesses DHS's efforts to address those lessons through 66 planned activities, and reports key participants' views of their experiences during Cyber Storm II in March 2008.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The GAO found that DHS identified eight lessons from Cyber Storm I and made progress in addressing them, but more remains to be done. Of the 66 activities DHS identified to address the lessons, 42 were completed and validated, 1 was reported as completed but not validated due to insufficient evidence, 16 were ongoing, and 7 were planned for the future. Key activities remained unfinished, and DHS had not established completion dates for activities reported as ongoing. Cyber Storm II participants observed both progress and continued challenges in building a national cyber response capability, and many of the challenges were similar to those identified during the first exercise. The GAO concluded that until DHS schedules and completes its corrective activities, the agency risks wasting resources on subsequent exercises that repeat the lessons learned in 2006.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The document reports the following figures: 18 critical infrastructure sectors; Cyber Storm I in February 2006 cost about $3.7 million and involved 8 federal departments, 3 agencies, 3 states, 4 foreign countries, 11 information technology companies, 7 electric companies, 1 banking and finance company, 2 airlines, and over 100 public and private agencies, associations, and corporations; Cyber Storm II in March 2008 cost about $6.4 million and involved 18 federal agencies, 9 states, 10 information sharing and analysis centers, 5 foreign countries, and over 40 industry representatives from the private sector. DHS identified 8 lessons and 66 activities: 42 were reported and validated as completed, 1 was reported as completed but not validated, 16 were ongoing, and 7 were planned for the future. DHS listed 121 activities to address lessons 1 through 8, with 55 repeating a prior activity. Per-lesson counts were: interagency coordination groups, 32 activities with 24 completed and 8 ongoing or planned; contingency planning, risk assessment, and roles and responsibilities, 15 activities with 8 completed and 7 ongoing or planned; integration of incidents across infrastructures, 16 activities with 9 completed and 7 ongoing or planned; access to information, 15 activities with 8 completed and 7 ongoing or planned; coordination of response activities, 15 activities with 11 completed and 4 ongoing or planned; strategic communications and public relations, 5 activities with 1 completed and 4 ongoing or planned; processes, tools, and technology, 12 activities with 8 completed and 4 ongoing or planned; and the exercise program, 11 activities with 9 completed and 2 ongoing or planned. The GAO concluded that DHS has completed over 60 percent of these activities, and DHS's comment letter reported that after receiving the draft report it completed additional items, raising the percentage of corrective actions completed to over 70 percent.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document makes one recommendation for executive action: the Secretary of Homeland Security should direct the Assistant Secretary for Cybersecurity and Communications to ensure the scheduling and completion of the corrective actions addressing lessons learned during Cyber Storm I before conducting the next Cyber Storm exercise. DHS concurred with the recommendation. The document also notes that federal policy requires DHS to develop and maintain a system to collect, analyze, and disseminate lessons learned, and that DHS's exercise program guidance requires planners to identify a list of corrective actions and track their implementation.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document does not settle whether the remaining corrective activities from Cyber Storm I will be completed before the next Cyber Storm exercise. DHS had not identified completion dates for activities reported as ongoing. DHS stated that end dates were not applicable for many remaining corrective actions because they were ongoing, long-term, or dependent on outside stakeholders, but the GAO found that most remaining activities were finite and could be associated with a time frame. The GAO did not modify the status of activities after DHS reported completing additional items because DHS had not provided sufficient evidence. The document also states that GAO's observations from Cyber Storm II participants are not intended to be generalized to other exercise participants, and that DHS planned to issue a report on what it learned from Cyber Storm II by the end of 2008.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report, GAO-08-852, issued June 27, 2008, reviews the Department of Homeland Security's risk-based methodology for allocating Homeland Security Grant Program funds, with a focus on changes from fiscal year 2007 to 2008 and the reasonableness of the fiscal year 2008 methodology. It covers the risk analysis model, the effectiveness assessment, the final allocation process, and the vulnerability element of the model, and concludes that the methodology is generally reasonable but that the current version's measure of vulnerability is limited.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: GAO found that for fiscal year 2008 DHS is primarily following the same methodology it used in fiscal year 2007, but changed the urban area boundaries used in the risk analysis model from a center city plus ten-mile radius to Census Bureau metropolitan statistical areas, as required by the 9/11 Act. DHS expanded the eligible urban areas to 60 UASI grantees, with the top seven highest-risk areas as Tier 1 and the other 53 risk-ranked areas as Tier 2. GAO found that DHS's risk-based methodology is generally reasonable: it includes the key risk elements of threat, vulnerability, and consequences; the consequence indices are reasonable; and the model's results are less sensitive to changes in assumptions than in the prior year. However, GAO found that the vulnerability element has limitations: DHS assigned every state and urban area a vulnerability score of 1.0, did not measure variations in vulnerability, and, as a practical matter, allowed final risk scores to be determined by threat and consequences scores. GAO also found that DHS could take an additional step to evaluate the reliability and validity of the peer review process, because DHS's analysis did not apply a generally-accepted method to ensure inter-rater reliability.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: Since 2002, DHS has distributed almost $20 billion through various DHS grant programs. In fiscal year 2007, DHS provided approximately $1.7 billion to states and urban areas through the Homeland Security Grant Program, and planned to distribute approximately $1.6 billion in fiscal year 2008. DHS used the same risk-based methodology to allocate $852 million in fiscal year 2008 under the Infrastructure Protection Program. In fiscal year 2007, 45 candidates were eligible for UASI funding: the 6 Tier 1 UASI grantees were allocated fifty-five percent of available funds, or approximately $410.8 million, and the 39 Tier 2 UASI grantees received forty-five percent, or approximately $336.1 million. In fiscal year 2008, there were 60 eligible UASI areas: the top 7 Tier 1 grantees received fifty-five percent of available funds, or approximately $429.9 million, and the remaining 53 Tier 2 grantees received forty-five percent, or approximately $351.7 million. The Threat Index accounted for 20 percent of the total risk score, and the Vulnerability and Consequences Index accounted for 80 percent. Within the consequences component, the Population Index was 40 percent, the Economic Index 20 percent, the National Infrastructure Index 15 percent, and the National Security Index 5 percent. The change to metropolitan statistical areas increased the total area of urban area footprints by almost 162,000 square miles; 3 urban areas lost square mileage, while the other areas increased their footprints by almost 2,700 square miles on average.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report's formal recommendation is that the Secretary of DHS instruct FEMA, I&A, and NPPD — the DHS components each responsible for aspects of the risk-based methodology used to allocate funds under the Homeland Security Grant Program — to formulate a method to measure vulnerability in a way that captures variations across states and urban areas, and apply this vulnerability measure in future iterations of the risk-based grant allocation model. FEMA and I&A concurred with this recommendation in email comments on the draft report. The report's February 2008 briefing also stated that DHS could take an additional step to evaluate the reliability and validity of the peer review process, such as having a sample of the same applications independently rated by multiple panels to provide a measure of inter-rater reliability.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that because information for assessing risks is imperfect, there is a degree of uncertainty in the information used for risk assessments, including what the threats are and how likely they are to be realized. It also states that DHS officials expressed limited confidence in the formula's ability to adequately represent threat, and that DHS program officials expressed concerns about their confidence in the existing threat information. The report notes that DHS did not provide details on what criteria its 'best fit' comparison for urban area footprints was based on. The report also notes that DHS is still developing a process to share threat assessments with UASI areas, including cross-state UASI areas, and that currently the assessments are transmitted only to DHS state representatives and state officials, who are responsible for sharing the information. In addition, the report notes that DHS identified resource constraints as a reason for not measuring inter-rater reliability in the peer review process.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: The document is a June 26, 2008 GAO report (GAO-08-854) to congressional committees reviewing recent use of the Defense Production Act of 1950 (DPA) since its 2003 reauthorization. Its scope covers DPA Titles I, III, and VII and seven agencies—Agriculture, Commerce, Defense, Energy, Health and Human Services, Homeland Security, and Transportation—in the areas of defense, energy, domestic emergency and disaster response and recovery, and critical infrastructure, plus agencies' response to reporting requirements on the economic impact of foreign offsets.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report finds that DOD is the primary user of DPA authorities, routinely applying priority ratings under Title I to almost all of its contracts, while civilian agencies have generally not used the authority and most would apply it only after a delivery problem has been identified. Civilian agencies responsible for civil transportation, health resources, and food and agriculture resources have not developed and implemented policies or guidance for using Title I; HHS and USDA are beginning to develop regulations modeled on DPAS, while DOT has not begun. Title III authority has been used almost exclusively for defense needs, and events triggering some Title VII authorities, such as the National Defense Executive Reserve and voluntary agreements, have not occurred. The report also finds that agencies have taken steps toward fulfilling offset reporting requirements, but Commerce's data limit analysis of the economic effects of offsets, and the DOD-chaired interagency team has consensus that adverse effects exist but not on best practices to address them.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The report is GAO-08-854, issued June 26, 2008, and is 36 pages long. DPA was reauthorized in 2003 through September 30, 2008. DOD places priority ratings on approximately 300,000 contracts annually. Since 2003, DHS reported authorizing or endorsing priority ratings 15 times, over half in support of critical infrastructure protection and restoration. Commerce reported approximately 180 Special Priorities Assistance actions since late 2003. DOT obtained a priority rating in 2002 to support procurement of approximately 1,800 Explosives Detection Systems machines by December 31, 2002. In Commerce's offset reports, 84 percent of the value of export contracts involving offsets submitted by prime contractors is in the aerospace industry, with no delineation among subsectors; the most recent annual report noted that its analysis did not include the potential effects of nearly $1 billion of technology transfer, training, and overseas investment offset transactions, nearly 24 percent of average annual offset transactions. For the 5-year period 1998 through 2002, Commerce requested documentation for only two weapon systems from each of 13 U.S. prime contractors rather than all nearly 700 weapon systems and components contracts, and the three-tier subcontractor survey had a less than 40 percent response rate. Offset regulations apply to agreements exceeding $5 million in value; they were first published in 1994 and have never been updated. The interagency team issued its third and final report in February 2007, held bilateral dialogue with Australia in May 2007 and multilateral dialogue with six other countries in November 2007, and set a goal of a preliminary statement by the latter half of 2008. DHS reported that establishing a voluntary agreement could take 21 to 50 days. DOD proposed statutory changes including reducing the waiting period for awarding contracts from 60 to 30 days and increasing the statutory limitation on Title III actions from $50,000,000 to $200,000,000. The report includes Title III project counts by fiscal year 2002 through 2008 (DOD-initiated and Congressionally requested, respectively: 2002 1 and 0, 2003 1 and 0, 2004 0 and 2, 2005 5 and 3, 2006 1 and 6, 2007 2 and 4, 2008 0 and 7) and Title III project funds including $163.91 million, $67.10 million, $20.41 million, $16.42 million, $16.20 million, $14.62 million, $13.96 million, $13.73 million, $11.44 million, $9.87 million, $9.18 million, $9.14 million, $8.37 million, $7.95 million, $5.42 million, $5.34 million, $5.30 million, $4.00 million, $3.38 million, $3.09 million, $2.84 million, $2.43 million, $1.91 million, $1.06 million, $0.88 million, and $31.38 million for projects with contracts not yet awarded, with a stated total of $449.3 million.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: GAO recommends that the Secretaries of Agriculture, Health and Human Services, and Transportation, in consultation with the Department of Commerce, develop and implement a system for using the priorities and allocations authority for food and agriculture resources, health resources, and civil transportation, respectively. GAO also recommends that the Secretaries of Agriculture, Energy, Health and Human Services, Homeland Security, and Transportation consider, in advance of an emergency, approving programs and placing priority ratings on contracts for items likely to be needed in an emergency. GAO additionally recommends that the Secretary of Commerce update regulations to request more specific industry information from prime contractors to improve the assessment of the economic effects of offsets. The report says USDA generally concurred with the findings and recommendations; HHS and DOT, in technical comments, indicated they will implement the recommendations.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report states that HHS is developing a priorities and allocations regulation but has no timeline for completion, while DOT officials said they have not yet begun developing regulations. The interagency working group reached consensus to pursue a statement of best practices for limiting the adverse effects of offsets, but participants identified challenges including a lack of agreement on terminology, and participating nations noted that producing such a statement would be difficult and time-consuming. The National Commission on Offsets produced only an interim report in 2001; its final report was never produced. The report also notes the difficulty of isolating offsets' effects from other factors; Commerce's employment analysis relies on aggregated defense aerospace data and excludes other defense sectors and aerospace subsectors; the 2004 employment analysis was limited by the survey response rate and subjective measurements; and BIS was reviewing data and methodology, with Commerce officials anticipating the outcome in the next annual report, but changes to the regulation would not affect data collection for that report. DOD officials noted statutory limitations, including the annual budget-cycle notification requirement creating a waiting period of up to one year and the 60-day waiting period for awarding contracts. FEMA had interim guidance on NDER units but had not activated its NDER and was assessing the need for it; DOE and DOT no longer have active NDER units, though officials expressed interest in restoring or re-establishing them.

audience.text: The report is addressed to the congressional committees listed: the Senate and House Committees on Armed Services, the Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs, and the House Committee on Financial Services; it supports congressional oversight and decision-making on DPA authorities and foreign offset reporting.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report to congressional committees examines how the Chemical Safety and Hazard Investigation Board (CSB) has responded to GAO and inspector general recommendations concerning its investigative gap, data quality problems, human capital problems, and accountability and management problems, and assesses the merits of the current oversight approach using an existing office of inspector general and alternative approaches. It concludes that improvements in CSB management and oversight are needed.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: Based on a performance audit conducted from October 2007 to May 2008, GAO finds that CSB has implemented some GAO and IG recommendations but has not fully addressed several critical recommendations, and problems in governance, management, and oversight persist. Specifically, the investigative gap persists, data quality problems continue, human capital problems persist, and accountability and management problems continue. GAO finds that CSB continues to fall short of its statutory mandate to investigate accidental releases that result, or have the potential to result, in a fatality, serious injury, or substantial property damage, and that Congress does not have accurate or comprehensive information about CSB's investigative gap or the resources needed to close it. GAO also finds that independent oversight from an existing IG remains the most effective way to help CSB address its continuing problems, provided the arrangement is made permanent and funding is provided to the IG for the function. CSB generally concurred with four of the six recommendations and disagreed with two, and disagreed with both matters for congressional consideration.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: CSB reported receiving notification of approximately 900 chemical accidents in calendar year 2007, of which 31 were serious or fatal events warranting CSB investigators. CSB was appropriated $9.4 million for fiscal year 2008 and had 39 staff as of January 30, 2008. Since fiscal year 2001, three IGs have provided oversight, and from fiscal year 2002 through 2007 inspectors general made 32 recommendations. In fiscal year 2007, CSB received notifications of 920 chemical accidents; approximately 35 included at least one fatality, and CSB investigated 1 of these. In fiscal year 2007, CSB investigated less than 1 percent (5 of 920) of accidents of which it was notified. In fiscal years 2006 and 2007, the accident-screening database recorded 822 and 920 total accidents, 38 and 35 accidents with fatalities, 9 and 8 deployments, 6 and 5 investigations, and 5 and 1 accidents with fatalities that CSB investigated. Using fiscal year 2002 data, the DHS IG reported in fiscal year 2004 that CSB deployed to 4 of 294 accidents that met statutory criteria; the briefing slides state CSB screened 613 accidents, about 294 met statutory criteria, and CSB deployed investigators to 4. NTSB's budget is approximately 8 times CSB's budget, and NTSB investigates 250 times as many accidents. In fiscal year 2006, CSB initiated 6 investigations with a budget of $9.1 million, while NTSB initiated 1,521 aviation accident investigations with a budget of $75.9 million; NTSB also completed 19 nonaviation accident investigations in fiscal year 2006. In an analysis of a subset of accidents involving fatalities and injuries, GAO found at least 5 accidents (about 6 percent of cases reviewed) where fatalities were not correctly recorded and 7 accidents (about 4 percent of cases reviewed) where injury data were missing. In fiscal year 2006, CSB reprogrammed compensation funds of $627,891 to other priorities, and in fiscal year 2007 it reprogrammed compensation funds of $407,383. In fiscal years 2006 and 2007, CSB hired 7 noninvestigative staff and 4 investigators, while 9 noninvestigative staff and 5 investigators left; 3 of the 5 investigators who left were senior investigators with 5 to 7 years of experience. Of 11 staff hired, 4 were investigators, and 3 of those 4 were interns. CSB has not paid a retention bonus to any employee since September 2002. Two of four intern investigators hired in fiscal years 2004 and 2005 left CSB, and one transferred to another office. CSB requested $10.6 million and 47 staff for fiscal year 2009, and $12.5 million and 60 staff in fiscal year 2000. Prior appropriations and staffing were $9.4 million and 39 staff in fiscal year 2008, $9.2 million and 41 staff in fiscal year 2006, $8.2 million and 40 staff in fiscal year 2004, and $8.0 million and 27 staff in fiscal year 2000. CSB stated that it currently obtains its financial and information security audits for about $60,000 a year.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: GAO recommends that the chairman of the Chemical Safety Board develop a plan to address the investigative gap and request the necessary resources from Congress to meet CSB's statutory mandate or seek an amendment to its statutory mandate; consider using the work of other entities, such as government agencies, companies, and contractors, subject to an assessment of the quality of their work, to a greater extent to maximize the board's limited resources; improve the quality of its accident-screening database by better controlling data entry and periodically sampling accident data to evaluate their consistency and completeness; publish a regulation requiring facilities to report all chemical accidents, as required by law, to better inform the agency of important details about accidents that it may not receive from current sources; consider reinstating the position of chief operating officer, with delegations of responsibility for establishing performance goals, holding program managers accountable for meeting those goals, and demonstrating improvement in the agency's ability to meet its statutory mandates over time; and use the Strategic Management of Human Capital portion of the President's Management Agenda to provide criteria for developing a comprehensive human capital plan, with input from investigators, that includes specific objectives and performance measures. GAO also proposes matters for congressional consideration: Congress may wish to consider amending CSB's authorizing statute or the Inspector General Act of 1978 to permanently give EPA's Inspector General the authority to serve as the oversight body for CSB, and Congress may wish to consider providing the EPA Inspector General with appropriations and staff allocations specifically for the audit function of CSB via a direct line in the EPA appropriation.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that the accident-screening database is sufficiently reliable only for making broad estimates of the total number of accidents and accidents with fatalities, and that its limitations include a lack of quality controls to ensure data are accurate and complete, especially with respect to fatalities. It also states that GAO did not evaluate the quality of CSB's investigative products issued to date, or the quality and effectiveness of its reports, recommendations, and promotion of preventive actions, because those evaluations were outside the scope of the mandate. GAO did not conduct a detailed evaluation of the oversight arrangements for the other 53 federal entities for comparison with CSB. The document also reports unresolved disagreements: CSB does not agree that its authorizing statute requires investigation of every chemical accident involving a fatality, serious injury, or substantial property damage or the potential for such consequences, while GAO continues to believe the law is clear; CSB disagrees that a reporting regulation is needed, while GAO disagrees with CSB's view; and CSB questioned the independence of the EPA IG, while GAO concluded the IG Act provides the requisite independence and the EPA IG poses no risk to CSB's independent evaluation of chemical accidents. In addition, the current IG arrangement is not permanent, and EPA IG officials told GAO they have no plans to conduct future program evaluations of CSB because they are allocating limited evaluation resources to other priorities within EPA.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) report to Congressional requesters assessing the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corporation's (PBGC) contracting function. It evaluates (1) the role contracting plays in PBGC's efforts to accomplish its mission, (2) the steps PBGC has taken to improve its acquisition infrastructure and develop a strategic approach to contracting, and (3) the steps PBGC has taken to improve its contract oversight processes to ensure accountability. The report includes recommendations for executive action by the Director of PBGC.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: Contracting plays a central role in helping PBGC achieve its mission and address unpredictable workloads. PBGC's workforce currently consists of about 800 federal employees and about 1,500 contract employees. From fiscal year 2000 through 2007, PBGC's contract spending increased steadily along with its overall budget and workload, and its use of contract employees has outpaced its hiring of federal employees. PBGC is taking steps to improve its acquisition infrastructure, but its Procurement Department is not yet part of PBGC's strategic decision-making process; for example, the Procurement Department is not included in corporate-level strategic planning and does not have a presence on PBGC's relevant strategic teams. PBGC has made improvements to contractor oversight since GAO's last report and has begun to implement performance-based contracting, which offers the potential for better contract outcomes but also creates new challenges for contract oversight and monitoring efforts. Most of PBGC's current contracts still lack performance incentives and methods to hold contractors accountable. PBGC agreed with most of GAO's recommendations but disagreed with the recommendation to reflect the importance of contracting and incorporate its vision for future contractor use in its strategic planning documents, and with the recommendation that its Director of Procurement should sit on certain specific corporate committees.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: PBGC insures pensions for more than 44 million workers in over 30,000 employer-sponsored defined benefit plans. In fiscal year 2007, roughly 611,000 beneficiaries received over $4.1 billion in benefit payments. PBGC showed an accumulated deficit of $14 billion for its single-employer program as of September 2007. PBGC's workforce currently consists of about 800 federal employees and about 1,500 contract employees. PBGC's budget increased from $165 million in fiscal year 2000 to $398 million in fiscal year 2007; contract spending increased from $122 million in fiscal year 2000 to $297 million in fiscal year 2007. Contracting represented 71 percent of PBGC's appropriated budget during fiscal years 2000 through 2007. PBGC had 763 federal employees in fiscal year 2000 and 811 in fiscal year 2007; contractor employees grew from 791 in fiscal year 2000 to 1,502 in fiscal year 2007, peaking at 1,768 in fiscal year 2006. PBGC administered 2,874 pension plans in fiscal year 2000 and 3,793 in fiscal year 2007; participants administered were 541,000 in fiscal year 2000 and 1,305,000 in fiscal year 2007. Pending benefit determinations were 168,886 in fiscal year 2000 and 356,022 in fiscal year 2007. PBGC contracts include managing $68 billion of assets. PBGC has awarded less than $150 million in service contract dollars in fiscal year 2008; only six contracts are performance based, representing a yearly cost of approximately $30 million, and PBGC is in the process of awarding an additional $20 million in performance-based contracts for field benefit administration offices. The Procurement Department had 2 of 12 contract specialist staff certified as of February 2007 and 9 of 12 certified by January 2008. A May 2007 staffing study found PBGC had 88 percent more transactions on average and 40 percent more contract dollars on average than four comparable agencies, but less than half the average number of contracting office staff. PBGC's agency comment letter states the Procurement Department's automated customer service questionnaire reflects a current customer satisfaction rate of 88 percent.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Director of PBGC revise its strategic plan and, in drafting the corporation's human capital strategic plan, reflect the importance of contracting and PBGC's use of contractors, project its vision of future contractor use, and better link staffing and contracting decisions at the corporate level. Specifically, the Director of PBGC should: include the Procurement Department in agency-wide strategic planning; ensure that the Procurement Director sits on PBGC's three strategic teams (the Operations Integration Board, the Budget and Planning Integration Team, and the Capital Planning for Information Technology Team); broaden the Procurement Department's May 2007 staffing study to include as part of PBGC's agency-wide acquisition workforce those positions outside of the Procurement Department that have a significant impact on procurement outcomes, and determine appropriate staffing levels for these positions; include in PBGC's human capital plan detailed plans for how contract support will be obtained; assess PBGC's contract information to determine if additional information is needed to support strategic acquisition management decisions, including more complete information on goods and services purchased, suppliers and spending patterns, and integrate contract spending information into PBGC's financial system; and develop metrics for PBGC's annual performance plan that document how the acquisition function supports PBGC's missions and goals. To improve contract management as PBGC implements a performance-based approach, the report recommends that the Director of PBGC provide comprehensive training on performance-based contracting for PBGC's Procurement Department staff, managers, and acquisition-related workforce; develop practices to help ensure accountability for Procurement Department staff carrying out contract monitoring responsibilities; and ensure that future contracts measure performance in terms of outcomes, provide incentives for the accomplishment of desired outcomes, and ensure payment of award fees only for excellent performance.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that it is still too early to tell what the effect of PBGC's new contracting policies will be. It also states that GAO did not conduct an independent assessment of PBGC's May 2007 staffing study to validate the study's results. Regarding oversight, the document notes that due to COTR work activities, not all site visits are being conducted as anticipated; only one to two are being conducted per office each year. It states the American Customer Service Index is not completely effective as an incentive mechanism because it does not report results for individual contractors and instead reports on contracts collectively. The document says PBGC's strategic plan only briefly mentions performance-based contracting, flexible staffing and metrics for specific contracts, does not provide measurable goals or time frames for converting contracts, and lacks key attributes of successful performance measures such as measurable targets with numerical goals. It also notes PBGC's workload depends on future economic conditions that are difficult to predict, and that a PBGC official said PBGC does not foresee large plan terminations and bankruptcies coming in 2008 or 2009, but there are a few plans it is monitoring that could have significant impact on PBGC.
