about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This is a U.S. Government Accountability Office (GAO) report to the Chairman and Ranking Member of the Subcommittee on Air and Land Forces, House Committee on Armed Services, dated August 15, 2008. It examines how the Department of Defense and the military services have managed acquisitions of tactical radios, focusing on how planned investments in key tactical radio systems changed over fiscal years 2003 through 2007, why those changes occurred, and what challenges will confront the services as they plan tactical radio investments for future capabilities. The report covers both legacy radios and the Joint Tactical Radio System (JTRS), including development delays, cost and performance problems, legacy-radio purchases driven by combat operations, and the need for a department-wide investment strategy.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: GAO found that DOD spent an estimated $12 billion on the development and production of tactical radios over the last 5 years, an amount comparable to estimated investments in the Army's Future Combat Systems ($10.4 billion) and the Navy's Virginia Class submarines ($10.8 billion) in the same period. Planned spending on tactical radios for fiscal years 2003 through 2007 was about $3.2 billion, but actual spending was about $8.3 billion, and it shifted away from procuring JTRS toward procuring tens of thousands of additional legacy radios. About $5.7 billion was actually spent on legacy radios, compared with a planned $235 million for Army and Marine Corps legacy radios, while about $2.5 billion was spent on JTRS development; no JTRS networking radios were produced or fielded during this time. GAO found that the change was due primarily to delays in the development and production of JTRS and to urgent demands for additional legacy radios to equip current forces, including combat operations in Iraq and Afghanistan, force modernization, and a change in the Army and Marine Corps concept of operations that calls for more radios per combat unit. Supplemental funding supplied an estimated $5.5 billion of the $6.1 billion the Army and Marine Corps received to procure legacy radios. The waiver and notification process for managing the transition from legacy radios to JTRS was not effective in tracking the nature and extent of tactical radio investments. Looking ahead, the report finds that JTRS must still overcome technology, size and power, and security architecture issues; that JTRS radios are significantly more costly than legacy radios; that the services have scaled back the number of JTRS radios they plan to buy; and that DOD does not have a strategy for balancing future tactical radio investments. DOD agreed with GAO's recommendations.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: DOD spent an estimated $12 billion on the development and production of tactical radios over the last 5 years. Estimated investments in the Army's Future Combat Systems were $10.4 billion and in the Navy's Virginia Class submarines were $10.8 billion during the same period. In 2002, DOD planned to invest close to $3 billion in JTRS over fiscal years 2003 through 2007: about $1 billion to develop and test the radios and about $2 billion to start procuring them. The Army and Marine Corps planned to spend only about $235 million between 2003 and 2007 on legacy radios for ground vehicles and soldiers and marines. Compared with the $3.2 billion that was slated to be spent on JTRS and the Army and Marine Corps legacy radios, about $8.3 billion was actually spent. Of this, about $5.7 billion was spent on legacy radios, while $2.5 billion was spent on JTRS development. The planned amounts were $0.24 billion for legacy radios and $2.93 billion for JTRS; actual amounts were $5.72 billion for legacy radios and $2.54 billion for JTRS. The Army spent approximately $4.1 billion on legacy radios, including $2.3 billion on SINCGARS radios and $1.8 billion on handheld and manpack radios; the Marine Corps spent $1.6 billion on a variety of tactical communication systems. Legacy radio spending was about 24 times what was planned. Supplemental funding supplied an estimated 90 percent, or $5.5 out of $6.1 billion, of the funding the Army and Marine Corps received to procure legacy radios. The annual base and supplemental budget figures for Army and Marine Corps tactical radios were: 2003, $122 million base and $0 supplemental; 2004, $109 million base and $225 million supplemental; 2005, $133 million base and $1,273 million supplemental; 2006, $111 million base and $2,273 million supplemental; and 2007, $114 million base and $1,754 million supplemental. In fiscal year 2008, the Army and Marine Corps requested an additional $3.3 billion in October 2007, and in March 2008 the Army informed Congress that it had overstated its request for SINCGARS funding by $1.7 billion, requesting funds for 170,756 more SINCGARS when only 56,000 were needed. The estimated cost to develop JTRS and its various program components increased from about $3.5 billion to almost $6 billion through fiscal year 2011. The production decision for the JTRS Ground Mobile Radio was delayed by 5 years, from 2005 to 2010, and the start of system development for the Airborne, Maritime, and Fixed Station radios was delayed by 2 years, from 2006 to 2008. The JTRS restructuring reduced the number of radio variants by half, from 26 to 13, and the number of waveforms by about two-thirds, from 32 to 11. Army Aviation planned to spend approximately $310 million between 2005 and 2013 on an alternate legacy radio system for helicopters. The Navy planned to spend approximately $50 million in research and development for modernization of the AN/ARC-210 radio. Some Army National Guard units were equipped at 65 to 75 percent of requirements. A typical Marine Corps rifle company of about 180 marines was equipped with 9 tactical radios prior to the war in Iraq and about 225 radios after. In September 2004, the Army estimated it would need an additional 66,166 SINCGARS receiver and transmitter units to support modularity. The Army's authorized acquisition objective for SINCGARS was 232,411 radio units in fiscal year 2002, 327,655 in 2004, 472,567 in 2005, 526,192 in 2007, and 581,000 in 2008; the Army bought 244,780 SINCGARS between 2003 and 2007. A fully configured vehicular SINCGARS radio costs about $20,000; the Enhanced Position Location Reporting System costs about $20,000 to $33,000; the 4-channel vehicular JTRS Ground Mobile Radio is about $220,000; the latest generation 1-channel AN/ARC-210 radio costs about $80,000; the 2-channel airborne JTRS radio is about $480,000; Handheld, Manpack, and Small Form Fit radios average about $27,000; and maritime and fixed station radios can exceed $1 million. The cost to retrofit and fully integrate JTRS networking capabilities into four Naval aircraft was estimated at about $868 million. Planned JTRS procurement quantities were 108,086 Ground Mobile Radios at Milestone B, 138,913 when the program was restructured in 2006, and 86,512 in 2008; 328,514 Handheld, Manpack, and Small Form Fit radios at Milestone B, 164,137 in 2006, and 95,551 in 2008; and 17,007 Airborne, Maritime, and Fixed Station radios in 2006 and 11,040 in 2008. The total planned JTRS quantity was 436,600 at Milestone B, 320,057 in 2006, and 193,103 in 2008. The Ground Mobile Radio quantity decreased by 20 percent, and the Handheld, Manpack, and Small Form Fit quantity decreased by 71 percent. The preliminary unit cost estimate for the JTRS Rifleman Radio is about $2,000, compared with the $8,700 unit cost of the small form factor C radio using military GPS, and the Army proposed an initial requirement for 100,000 or more Rifleman Radios. The Ground Mobile Radio program's Nunn-McCurdy unit-cost breach, declared in November 2007, reflected an increase in program acquisition unit cost of about 24 percent above the 2002 baseline. The Multifunctional Information Distribution System-JTRS program had a schedule slip of almost 12 months. The planned expansion would add more than 74,000 soldiers to the Army by 2013 and 27,000 marines to the Marine Corps by 2011.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: GAO recommended that the Secretary of Defense develop a comprehensive strategy and implementation plan for making sound investment decisions for tactical radios that is based on operational architectures defining the communications and networking functions needed on the battlefield, assesses and prioritizes the capabilities and requirements needed in the near and long term, sets bounds for the funding committed to address these needs, lays out an effective migration and fielding plan for delivering capabilities to the warfighter, and identifies contingencies in case there are further problems and delays with JTRS. GAO also recommended that the Secretary of Defense reinvigorate the tactical radio notification and waiver process to provide department-wide insight into the continued procurement of legacy and interim radios, with consideration given to ensuring that clear guidance and procedures are developed and communicated across the department. The Department of Defense agreed with both recommendations in its comments on the draft report.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report states that GAO was unable to obtain plans or actual procurement information from the Navy or Air Force because, according to Navy and Air Force officials, these services do not centrally procure radios, and that GAO was able to identify tactical radio investments only in Army and Marine Corps budget documents. It states that notifications submitted by the services through the waiver and notification process were inconsistent and did not reflect all tactical radio procurements that took place over the past several years, and that the input the services provided for the new migration and fielding plan was not linked to operational architectures and lacked sufficient detail on current and future requirements and funding priorities. The report also states that it will not be known whether JTRS's technical challenges, including size, weight, power, thermal management, and security certification requirements, can be overcome until major test and evaluation events are conducted in the next few years. It notes that the 2003 JTRS migration plan has not yet been updated despite being intended as a living and evolving document, that previous plans are outdated, and that a comprehensive plan balancing needs with available resources and identifying contingencies is still lacking. The report also notes that the pre- and post-restructuring components of the Handheld, Manpack, and Small Form Fit program did not lend themselves to direct comparison for schedule purposes, and that DOD did not provide additional information on the measures it is taking that are consistent with its recommendations.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a September 12, 2008, GAO report to congressional requesters updating the status of the planned new federal courthouse for the U.S. District Court in Los Angeles. It covers the causes and effects of project delays, the near-tripling of estimated costs, and the options available for the future of the project, including three GSA proposals and a restart of the planning process.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report's own findings are that the L.A. courthouse project has been delayed by GSA's decision to design a courthouse larger than Congress authorized, slow scope-reduction decisions by GSA and the judiciary, unforeseen construction cost escalation, and procurement problems. GSA's projected occupancy moved from fiscal year 2006 to fiscal year 2014, an 8-year delay, and estimated costs to house the L.A. Court have nearly tripled to over $1.1 billion, making the authorized 41-courtroom courthouse unachievable with available funding. GSA has spent $33.2 million and about $366.45 million remains. Court operational inefficiencies, space deficits, and security problems at the Spring Street building persist. GSA has developed eight proposals since 2000, with three still under consideration and a fourth option of restarting the planning process, and the report states there is no consensus among stakeholders and the process is deadlocked.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: GSA projected occupancy in fiscal year 2006 in 2000, fiscal year 2009 in 2003, fiscal year 2010 in 2004, and fiscal year 2014 in 2008, an 8-year delay. Congress appropriated approximately $400 million: $35.25 million in fiscal year 2001 for site acquisition and design, $50 million in fiscal year 2004 for construction, and $314.4 million in fiscal year 2005 for construction of a 41-courtroom building. GSA spent $16.3 million on design and $16.9 million on site acquisition and preparation; the report and briefing state GSA has spent $33.2 million in total, leaving about $366.45 million. The authorized project was a 41-courtroom, 1,016,300-square-foot courthouse; GSA designed a 54-courtroom, 1,279,650-square-foot building. Current estimates for a courthouse of similar scope exceed $1.1 billion. Each day of additional delay costs about $54,000, and every 44 days of delay costs as much as one 2,400-square-foot district courtroom. The three options under consideration are: a 36-courtroom, 45-chamber building with 4 added Roybal courtrooms, estimated at $1.1 billion with $733.6 million in additional appropriations needed, 74 total courtrooms, completion in 2014; a 20-courtroom, 20-chamber building with 12 added Roybal courtrooms, estimated at $701.1 million with $301.5 million additional, 66 total courtrooms, completion in 2014; and adding 13 Roybal courtrooms with 17 Spring Street courtrooms retained and security upgraded, estimated at $648.4 million with $282.1 million additional, 64 total courtrooms (some below design standards), completion in 2016. The Spring Street building has 32 courtrooms, 11 of which do not meet minimum design standards; the Roybal building has 34 courtrooms: 10 district, 6 magistrate, and 18 bankruptcy. Main report Table 2 space deficits are: court, chamber, and support space 133,838 square feet current and 197,613 projected for 2011; probation 3,292 and 6,426; district clerk's office 6,165 and 25,696; jury assembly 9,635 and 9,650. The appendix I briefing lists the projected 2011 probation deficit as 8,144 square feet. Construction cost escalation in the L.A. market went as high as 16 percent in 2006. GSA estimated $50 billion in public construction projects in the L.A. market. GSA's repair and maintenance backlog is $6.6 billion. USMS security logs showed a five-fold increase in suspicious activities in L.A. federal courthouses from 2004 to 2007.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report makes no recommendation. It states, "We are not advocating any of these options." It notes that GSA will need to obtain congressional approval to move forward on any plan, and that all options currently under consideration would require approval of a new prospectus and an estimated appropriation of from $282.1 million to $733.6 million. It also presents a fourth option for GSA and the judiciary to restart the planning process, with the remaining $366.5 million potentially remaining for the project or being transferred or rescinded for other purposes such as GSA's $6.6 billion repair and maintenance backlog.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states there is no consensus among stakeholders on how to proceed and that the current process is deadlocked. It says GSA has developed numerous proposals and it is difficult to know which one it believes is the best solution. It notes that Option 3's cost estimates were based on the assumption that work would have started by now, which has not occurred. It notes that the success of the 20-courtroom option relies on GSA obtaining authorization and appropriation to add courtrooms in Roybal, without which the court could be split among three buildings. It also notes that GSA and judiciary officials disagree about the reasons for the increased project scope. The report states that the cost-of-delay estimate does not include all support space associated with courtroom operations, and that the estimates for the 36- and 20-courtroom options do not include site and design work already completed. It also identifies uncertainty about what support operations would move under the 20-courtroom option, and notes that assessing the validity of GSA's project budget and schedule was outside the scope of the report.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a July 31, 2008 GAO report to congressional requesters on federal information technology project rebaselining. It examines the extent and primary reasons for rebaselining among the 778 major IT projects the 24 major federal agencies planned to fund in fiscal year 2008, and whether agencies' rebaselining policies are sound relative to best practices in GAO's draft Cost Assessment Guide.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The document's own findings are that an estimated 48 percent of the federal government's major IT projects funded in fiscal year 2008 have been rebaselined; of those rebaselined, 51 percent were rebaselined at least twice and about 11 percent were rebaselined 4 or more times. The most common reasons for the most recent rebaseline were changes in project requirements, objectives, or scope (55 percent) and changes in funding stream (44 percent). Rebaselining can produce significant cost and schedule changes, as in the Coast Guard's Rescue 21 system, projected to have cost increases of 184 percent and schedule delays of 5 years. The document also finds that although all 24 major agencies have rebaselining policies, none are fully consistent with the five best practices in GAO's draft Cost Assessment Guide; describing the process for developing a new baseline and requiring validation of the new baseline were addressed least. The document attributes the variation in policies in part to OMB's lack of guidance specifying what elements agencies' rebaselining policies should include.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: The federal government plans to spend about $70 billion on information technology projects during fiscal year 2008, with the bulk on 778 major projects at 24 major agencies. The survey sample was 180 projects, with a 99 percent response rate. The document estimates that about 48 percent of major IT projects have been rebaselined; figure 1 labels the estimated percentage as Rebaselined: 49% and Not rebaselined: 51%. Of rebaselined projects, 51 percent were rebaselined at least twice and about 11 percent were rebaselined 4 times or more. The most commonly cited reason for the most recent rebaseline was change in project requirements, objectives, or scope, at 55 percent; change in funding stream was cited at 44 percent. The document's table 2 also reports original baseline was inaccurate at 14 percent, cost or schedule overruns due to project performance at 4 percent, cost or schedule overruns due to contractor performance at 4 percent, and other at 41 percent. In table 3, cost and schedule changes for rebaselined projects (dollars in millions) are given as: NPOESS original cost $7000, cost after rebaseline(s) $12500, dollar change $5500, percent change 79%, original completion date 2018, completion date after rebaseline 2026, delay 8 years; Navy Enterprise Resource Planning original cost $1993, cost after rebaseline(s) $2445, dollar change $452, percent change 23%, original completion date Jun. 2011, completion date after rebaseline Aug. 2013, delay 2.2 years; FAA Standard Terminal Automation Replacement System original cost $940, cost after rebaseline(s) $2770, dollar change $1830, percent change 195%, original completion date Oct. 2005, completion date after rebaseline Dec. 2007, delay 2.2 years; FAA Wide Area Augmentation System original cost $1001, cost after rebaseline(s) $3340, dollar change $2339, percent change 234%, original completion date Aug. 1999, completion date after rebaseline Dec. 2008, delay 9.3 years; US Coast Guard Rescue 21 original cost $250, cost after rebaseline(s) $711, dollar change $461, percent change 184%, original completion date 2006, completion date after rebaseline 2011, delay 5 years.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The document recommends that the Director of the Office of Management and Budget issue guidance for rebaselining policies that would include a minimum set of key elements, taking into consideration the criteria used in this report, and that each of the heads of the 24 major agencies direct the development of comprehensive rebaselining policies that address the weaknesses GAO identified. No other recommendations are made in the document.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that the survey estimates are subject to sampling error: all proportion estimates from the sample have 95 percent confidence intervals within plus or minus 11 percentage points, unless otherwise noted, because each sample could have provided different estimates. It notes that percentages for reasons for rebaselining do not total 100 percent because multiple reasons could be provided. It also states that OMB has not established specific criteria to evaluate agencies' earned value management policies, and that agencies' policies vary in part because no guidance specifies what elements they should include. The document does not settle whether agencies will implement the recommendations.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a GAO report (GAO-08-930, September 10, 2008) to congressional committees on DOD planning for reposturing of U.S. forces from Iraq, i.e., the drawdown and realignment of forces, basing, and resources. It focuses on the logistical organizations and processes supporting redeployment of units and retrograde of materiel and equipment from Iraq. It examines when planning began and the assumptions behind it, whether DOD has established roles and responsibilities for managing retrograde, and identifies issues DOD needs to consider in developing a comprehensive reposturing plan.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report finds that various defense commands began reposture planning separately in fall 2007, but their efforts were uncoordinated until a May 2008 logistics summit at Camp Arifjan, Kuwait, which produced an MNF-I logistics reposture order and a working group. Planning rests on three assumptions: reposturing will be based on MNF-I and Department of State assessments; there will be sufficient lead time to refine plans once an order with a timetable and force posture is issued; and reposturing will be deliberate and gradual, predicated on a 180-day unit redeployment template and a sustained flow of no more than 2.5 brigades' worth of equipment and materiel out of Iraq each month. The report also finds that DOD, CENTCOM, and the military services have not clearly established roles and responsibilities for the retrograde process: no single organization has command authority over the theater property and retrograde support teams, until recently ARCENT lacked command authority over the two Army field support brigades responsible for most equipment, and data systems used in retrograde are incompatible despite an identified fix. It identifies nine issues DOD needs to consider: hazardous materials and waste and property disposition guidance; contractor reposturing plans; accountability for contractor-managed government-owned property; restrictive conditions on Kuwait and neighboring facilities; wash rack and customs inspector availability; transportation and convoy security capacity and route limits; mental health provider access; home-station infrastructure; and training and equipment reset requirements. DOD has begun to address these issues but none are fully addressed. DOD partially concurred with the first recommendation and fully concurred with the second.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: As of April 26, 2008, there were approximately 149,400 DOD contractors and, as of July 1, 2008, approximately 147,400 U.S. troops deployed in support of Operation Iraqi Freedom; DOD officials reported these forces were located on approximately 311 installations, with some more than 500 miles from Kuwait. According to DOD officials, approximately 80 percent of equipment used by U.S. troops in Iraq is theater provided equipment; as of March 2008 this pool totaled approximately 173,000 major end items worth approximately $16.5 billion. As of May 2008, DOD officials reported the equivalent of 47 brigades' worth of materiel and equipment in Iraq over some 311 installations, of which approximately 80 percent was theater provided equipment, approximately 582,000 pieces worth about $15.5 billion. As of summer 2007 there were more than 60,000 materiel containers in Iraq and over 127,000 short-tons of ammunition in Iraq and Kuwait. In January 2007 the President announced a surge of 5 additional brigades, bringing brigade combat teams in Iraq to 20; the MNF-I commander recommended drawdown from 20 to 15 brigade combat teams and a 45-day period of consolidation and evaluation after July 2008. Reposture planning assumes a 180-day unit redeployment process and a sustained flow of no more than 2.5 brigades' worth of equipment and materiel out of Iraq each month, based on a model that the theater infrastructure can sustain deployment and redeployment of no more than a total of five brigades' worth per month. On May 16, 2008, 177 pieces of theater provided equipment rolling stock were idle in Kuwait awaiting disposition instructions, some since March 2008, and over 2,100 non-rolling stock items were also idle. There is at least $3.5 billion worth of contractor-managed government-owned property in Iraq, including $3.37 billion under LOGCAP. The donation threshold for excess U.S.-owned personal property in Iraq was increased from $5,000 to $10,000 in October 2007 and from $10,000 to $15,000 in June 2008. An Army analysis indicated approximately 85 percent of contractor-acquired government-owned property in Iraq should be transferred, sold, or scrapped in Iraq, with the remaining 15 percent sold or reused elsewhere. There are 211 wash racks in Kuwait, 81 at Camp Arifjan and 130 at Kuwait Naval Base, of which only 100 at the naval base are useable because 30 lack necessary filters; washing a large vehicle takes 40 to 80 hours and a smaller vehicle 4 to 8 hours. An alternate regional port allowed retrograde of only 20 to 30 percent of nonsensitive Marine Corps materiel because of restrictions. Closing the smallest installations takes 1 to 2 months, while closing a complex installation such as Balad Air Force Base, with approximately 24,000 inhabitants, could take longer than 18 months. DLA rerouted 194 of 200 containers in one instance, and manifest information for equipment does not reach the 401st Army Field Support Brigade until 24 to 48 hours after a vessel sails. Officials from the 1st Cavalry Division said their brigade combat teams would not have necessary training equipment until 6 to 9 months after returning from Iraq.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Secretary of Defense, in consultation with CENTCOM and the military departments, take steps to clarify the chain of command over logistical operations in support of the retrograde effort, addressing both the Army field support brigades and the theater property and retrograde support teams, and correct the incompatibility weaknesses in the various data systems used to maintain visibility over equipment and materiel while in transit. It also presents a matter for congressional consideration: Congress may wish to consider directing DOD to include in its briefings under the National Defense Authorization Act for Fiscal Year 2008 specific details on the status of its reposturing planning and how it intends to mitigate specific reposturing issues identified in the report. The report notes DOD partially concurred with the first recommendation and fully concurred with the second.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report states that the pace and overall extent of reposturing has yet to be determined; that DOD's rate-of-flow model may be a useful planning tool but should not be used to predict how long it would take to retrograde all equipment and materiel in Iraq because actual amounts vary by brigade and several identified issues are not accounted for by the model; that time and cost estimates for closing bases are difficult to estimate without a U.S.-Iraq bilateral agreement on base closures, and as of July 18, 2008 no such agreement existed; and that home station issues such as mental health, infrastructure, and training and equipment reset need to be explored further. It also notes that as of May 2008 there was no agreed-upon definition for retrograde; that CENTCOM's June 2008 designation of ARCENT as having operational control over the 401st and 402nd Army Field Support Brigades had not been evaluated by GAO; and that an Army Sustainment Command order to fix data incompatibility had not been implemented for reasons that were not made clear. The report says DOD has begun to address the nine identified issues but none have been fully addressed.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report, issued July 3, 2008, to the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, describes a covert undercover operation in which GAO created two fictitious durable medical equipment, prosthetics, orthotics, and supplies (DMEPOS) suppliers, applied for Medicare billing numbers, and completed electronic test billing, in order to expose weaknesses in CMS's DMEPOS supplier screening process. It also presents four closed South Florida fraud cases obtained from the HHS Inspector General and describes CMS's corrective actions, including new accreditation requirements and proposed changes to the 25 supplier standards.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: GAO's covert testing found that CMS approved both fictitious DMEPOS storefronts GAO created, even though the companies had no clients and no inventory. CMS and NSC initially denied the applications because GAO had not demonstrated compliance with Standard 4, on the capacity to fill orders from inventory or through contracts, and Standard 14, on repairing or replacing rented items, but they accepted phony wholesale-supplier contracts and corrective action plans, performed only limited verification, and issued Medicare billing numbers for both companies. GAO then successfully completed Medicare's test billing process for the Virginia office by submitting 27 claims with no errors; it did not complete test billing for Maryland because the necessary passwords from CMS did not arrive by June 2008. GAO also reviewed closed HHS IG fraud cases showing fraudulent DMEPOS suppliers used stolen beneficiary and physician identification numbers to bill millions of dollars, including one company that billed $4.4 million and received $2.2 million. GAO concluded that the fraud prevention controls in place during the investigation were not effective and that a simple paperwork review is not sufficient.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: Medicare pays for care on behalf of almost 42 million elderly and certain disabled beneficiaries. In December 2006, the HHS Inspector General visited 1,581 DMEPOS suppliers in South Florida and found that almost one-third had no office at the address they provided Medicare. CMS estimated that from April 2006 through March 2007, $1 billion of the $10 billion in payments Medicare made for DMEPOS supplies were improper. GAO set up one company in Maryland (Zone A) and one in Virginia (Zone C). The offices rented for approximately $1,000 per month; online registration cost about $400 per supplier; and GAO purchased approximately $3 million worth of general liability insurance at a cost of $550 annually. The Maryland application ran from May 2007 to an approval effective February 13, 2008; the Virginia application ran from July 2007 to an approval retroactive to September 28, 2007. On May 14, 2008, GAO submitted a test file of 27 claims for $6,876.34 with no errors; the test billing requirement was at least 25 claims that were 95 percent error-free. In the case studies, one supplier submitted about $1.5 million in claims from January 1, 2006 through April 30, 2007 and was paid $372,286; another submitted claims in excess of $5.5 million from October 2006 through March 2007 and received about $77,000; another billed $4.4 million for undelivered supplies from March through July 2006 and was paid about $2.2 million; and another billed over $1 million from July 2005 through October 2006, was paid over $500,000, and bought beneficiary numbers illegally for $45 each. Sentences and restitution in the case studies included 30 months imprisonment and $372,286 restitution; 37 months imprisonment, over $70,000 restitution, and forfeiture of a Miami home and Rolls Royce; 4 years imprisonment, 3 years probation, a $100 fee, and $2.2 million restitution; and 2 years imprisonment, 3 years probation, and $702,186 restitution. The 25 supplier standards include a liability insurance requirement of at least $300,000. The report also notes that suppliers submitting enrollment applications on or after March 1, 2008, had to be accredited, with accreditation deadlines of January 1, 2009, for first-time enrollers between January 1 and February 29, 2008, and September 30, 2009, for suppliers enrolled before January 1, 2008, and that CMS's competitive bidding program had chosen suppliers in 10 Metropolitan Statistical Areas and was scheduled to begin July 1, 2008.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: This document makes no formal recommendations. It reports that CMS stated it is implementing new supplier requirements, including the accreditation process and the revisions and additions to the 25 standards proposed in January 2008, and that CMS acknowledged the covert testing illustrates gaps in oversight that still require improvement and said it would continue to work to strengthen the DMEPOS enrollment process.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that GAO used only fictitious Medicare beneficiaries and physician identification numbers found on the Internet to complete test billing and did not submit actual claims or compromise the provider status of legitimate physicians. It did not complete test billing for its Maryland office because it did not receive the necessary passwords from CMS by the close of the investigation in June 2008. It says that, based on review of HHS IG case studies, GAO believes that if the operation had continued it could have fraudulently billed Medicare for substantial sums, potentially reaching millions, but this is presented as a belief rather than a demonstrated outcome. The report also notes that NSC's acceptance of the phony wholesale suppliers was 'to our knowledge,' and concludes that CMS's additional actions will only be successful if those tasked with ensuring compliance exercise due diligence when conducting screenings and inspections.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a U.S. Government Accountability Office report, GAO-08-976, issued September 11, 2008, titled 'Veterans Health Administration: Improvements Needed in Design of Controls over Miscellaneous Obligations.' It reviews how the Veterans Health Administration used miscellaneous obligations during fiscal year 2007, focusing on the approximately $6.9 billion in miscellaneous obligations made by 129 VHA stations, and whether Department of Veterans Affairs policies and procedures were designed to provide adequate controls over the authorization and use of those obligations.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report finds that VHA used miscellaneous obligations extensively for mission-related activities in fiscal year 2007 and that VA policies and procedures were not designed to provide adequate controls over their use with respect to oversight by contracting officials, segregation of duties, and supporting documentation. These control design flaws were confirmed in case studies at Pittsburgh, Cheyenne, and Kansas City and increase the risk of fraud, waste, and abuse at the 129 VHA stations using miscellaneous obligations in fiscal year 2007. In the 42 miscellaneous obligations reviewed at the three case-study locations, none had documented approval by contracting officials, 30 had inadequate segregation of duties, 8 had incomplete purpose descriptions, 20 had blank vendor fields, and 16 had blank contract fields. The report also finds that over 88,000 (69 percent) of 127,070 miscellaneous obligations did not include vendor information, accounting for over $5 billion of the $6.9 billion, and that 145 miscellaneous obligations for over $30.2 million appeared to be used to procure items such as passenger vehicles, furniture and fixtures, office equipment, and medical, dental, and scientific equipment. New guidance issued in May 2008 offered some improvement but did not fully address the three problem areas, and VA attorneys had not reviewed the policies.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: In fiscal year 2007, the IFCAP database showed nearly 132,000 miscellaneous obligations with a total value of nearly $9.8 billion were created: VHA had 127,070 obligations totaling $6.9 billion, or 70 percent of total dollar value, and VA's Central Office had 4,839 obligations totaling $2.9 billion, or 30 percent, for a total of 131,909 obligations and $9.8 billion. Of VHA's $6.9 billion, about $3.8 billion, or 55.1 percent, was for services including fee-basis physician, nursing, dental, hospitalization stays, research, and prosthetic repair; $1.4 billion, or 20.4 percent, was for supplies including drugs, medicines, hospital supplies, blood products, and prosthetic supplies; $628 million, or 9.1 percent, was for rent, communications, and utilities; $553 million, or 8 percent, was for state homes and homeless veteran support; $301 million, or 4.4 percent, was for transportation of persons and things; and $210 million, or 3 percent, was for other items. VHA officials had disclosed that $4.8 billion, or 56 percent, of the reported $8.6 billion in procurements through the third quarter of fiscal year 2007 had been done using miscellaneous obligations. The case studies reviewed 42 miscellaneous obligations totaling $36,045,896: Pittsburgh had 14 obligations worth $6,694,853; Cheyenne had 11 obligations worth $2,076,648; and Kansas City had 17 obligations worth $27,274,395. In the segregation-of-duties analysis, 15 obligations involved one official performing two of four functions, 13 involved three of four functions, and 2 involved all four functions; 30 total had inadequate segregation of duties and 12 had adequate segregation. Other cited amounts include a $200,000 miscellaneous obligation at VA Boston that was requested, approved, and obligated by the same fiscal official; 12 Pittsburgh obligations totaling about $673,000 for University of Pittsburgh Medical Center laboratory services; about $141,000 for livers for transplant patients with a stated standardized price of $21,800; about $103,000 for utilities in Cheyenne; about $22,000 in Cheyenne employee grievance settlements; over $1.3 million and over $53,000 examples with incomplete purpose fields; $106,400 and $108,400 for clinic services estimates; $200,000 for Kirksville clinic services; and $8.6 million for Warrensburg Veteran's Home services. In fiscal year 2007, VA received appropriations of over $77 billion, including over $35 billion for health care and approximately $41.4 billion for other benefits, and Congress appropriated more than $87 billion for VA in fiscal year 2008.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Secretary of Veterans Affairs, in conjunction with VA's Office of General Counsel, develop and implement policies and procedures consistent with federal appropriations law and internal control standards that establish a process for the review of miscellaneous obligations by contracting officials, including requiring appropriate documentation that the review has occurred; segregate duties for creating, approving, and recording miscellaneous obligations, for the certification and payment of invoices, and for the receipt of the resulting goods or services; document the purposes, vendors, and contract numbers of miscellaneous obligations; and establish an oversight mechanism to ensure that these control policies and procedures are fully and effectively implemented. The Deputy Secretary of Veterans Affairs concurred with these recommendations and identified specific actions VA plans to take.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report states that it did not review VHA's procurement or service authorization processes. It could not reconcile IFCAP miscellaneous obligations to VA's Financial Management System because FMS does not identify the method used to obligate funds. The case-study results were based on a nongeneralizable sample of 42 obligations and cannot be projected to the overall population of fiscal year 2007 miscellaneous obligations. The report found no examples of fraudulent or otherwise improper purchases, but its work was not specifically designed to identify such cases or estimate their full extent. It did not verify that VHA officials were properly following the Medicare fee schedule, and it could not confirm that VHA was properly billed for or properly authorized the Pittsburgh liver procurement because officials could not provide a copy of the contract or the standardized pricing schedule. The report also notes that the May 2008 guidance did not address segregation of duties and did not establish an oversight mechanism, and that VA attorneys had not reviewed the policies to help ensure compliance with applicable appropriations law and other requirements.

audience.text: The report is addressed to the Chairman and Ranking Member of the Subcommittee on Oversight and Investigations, Committee on Veterans' Affairs, House of Representatives, to support their oversight of VHA's internal controls over miscellaneous obligations.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a GAO performance audit report, GAO-08-981R, issued August 15, 2008, on DOD's programs to promote positive working relationships between reservists and their employers. It examines (1) the extent to which DOD has taken steps to inform reservists of their obligations and responsibilities to provide timely notification to employers of a call to active duty, (2) DOD's initiatives to promote positive working relations between reservists and employers, and (3) whether there has been a reduction in hiring of reservists because of increased use of reservists after September 11, 2001, or because of changes in DOD policy. The audit was conducted from April 2008 through August 2008 and drew on DOD policy and guidance, Status of Forces Surveys, interviews with DOD officials and 11 employers selected from a nonprobability sample, and 10 focus groups with 50 reservists in Kentucky, North Carolina, and Virginia.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: DOD has taken steps to inform reservists of their obligations and responsibilities to provide advance notice to civilian employers, including DOD Instruction 1205.12 and ESGR outreach and education, but it does not collect data to assess the effectiveness of these efforts; its Status of Forces Surveys do not contain questions on the amount or type of notice reservists provide to employers. Focus groups found that some reservists provided only verbal notice, and some reservists said they would provide no more than 30 days' notice regardless of how much formal or informal notice they had received from DOD. DOD has used ESGR as its focal point for a strategic approach with many outreach initiatives, but ESGR lacks an established annual performance plan, a follow-up mechanism to maintain employer relationships after statements of support are signed, and an outreach program specific to small businesses. GAO was unable to determine the extent of any reduction in the hiring of reservists since September 11, 2001, because DOD and the Department of Labor lack data on this issue, and the available focus groups and employer interviews were based on nonprobability samples and are not generalizable. DOD partially concurred with the three final recommendations.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: Since September 11, 2001, DOD has relied on more than 650,000 members of the National Guard and Reserve. In fiscal year 2007, more than 67,000 employers and approximately 235,000 reservists were briefed on USERRA and ESGR services, and ESGR field committees briefed 68,803 employers. In fiscal year 2007, more than 20,644 employers signed statements of support, 15,124 employers were nominated for the Patriot Award, and more than 1,000 reservists nominated their employers for the Freedom Award. ESGR has a budget of approximately $13.1 million for fiscal year 2008, and operates through more than 4,500 volunteers in 56 committees, with 36 military employees, 28 civilian employees, 8 contractors, and 94 contractor field support personnel. According to the 2006 Status of Forces Survey, an estimated 79 percent of responding reserve component members said they had been briefed on USERRA at least once. According to the 2007 Status of Forces Survey, an estimated 76 percent of reservists had received an informal alert notice; of those, an estimated 77 percent received notice of 30 days or more; and an estimated 47 percent reported receiving written, formal orders 30 days or more prior to having to report for active duty. A November 2007 DOD report to Congress found that nearly 70 percent of employers of selected reservists have fewer than 100 employees. ESGR's August 22, 2007, strategic plan set a goal to obtain statements of support from all identified civilian employers of reservists by 2011, equating to an average of 20 percent of these employers in each year of the period covered by the plan. In DOD's written comments, ESGR Ombudsman Service data show total contacts increased from 5,298 in fiscal year 2005 to 7,765 in fiscal year 2006, 13,116 in fiscal year 2007, and 8,575 in fiscal year 2008 as of June 30; actual cases decreased from 4,682 in fiscal year 2005 to 3,152 in fiscal year 2006, 2,374 in fiscal year 2007, and 1,988 in fiscal year 2008 as of June 30; and statements of support increased from 10,909 in fiscal year 2005 to 11,396 in fiscal year 2006, 20,644 in fiscal year 2007, and 27,770 in fiscal year 2008 as of June 30.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: The report recommends that the Secretary of Defense direct the Under Secretary of Defense for Personnel and Readiness to take three actions: (1) establish an annual performance plan that develops and facilitates the implementation of performance measures on how well ESGR is achieving its goals, (2) conduct regular and recurring follow-up activities on outreach efforts to maintain positive working relationships with employers who have previously signed statements of support, and (3) develop initiatives to specifically conduct outreach efforts to small businesses that employ reservists. The report also notes that a fourth draft recommendation, to include questions in DOD's Status of Forces Surveys on the amount and form of notification reservists provide to employers, was omitted from the final report because Defense Manpower Data Center officials said they were planning to include such questions in subsequent surveys, and GAO encouraged full implementation of that initiative.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report states that GAO was unable to determine the extent to which there has been a reduction in the hiring of reservists caused by the increase in the use of reservists after September 11, 2001, or caused by changes in DOD's policies concerning reservists, due to a lack of available data. It also states that even if a reduction in hiring had occurred, GAO could not determine what factors contributed to the decline. The report notes that the employer interviews and reservist focus groups were based on nonprobability samples and the results are not generalizable to the general population of reservist employers or reservists. It also states that, given ESGR's numerous outreach programs and efforts, it is difficult to establish a direct causal link between these efforts and their effectiveness, and that DOD does not know whether its efforts are helpful in informing reservists of their USERRA responsibilities or enabling employers to receive advance notification of deployments.

audience.text: The report is addressed to the congressional committees listed in the document: the Senate Committee on Armed Services, the Senate Committee on Small Business and Entrepreneurship, the House Committee on Armed Services, and the House Committee on Small Business, as directed by the Military Reservists and Veteran Small Business Reauthorization and Opportunity Act of 2008.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This GAO report, issued August 25, 2008, examines continuing debris removal and disposal issues in the New Orleans area nearly three years after Hurricane Katrina. It describes key plans and practices that federal and state agencies are using to oversee debris removal and disposal, enforcement actions taken related to Katrina debris, and actions by the Louisiana Department of Environmental Quality and the Environmental Protection Agency in response to potential environmental issues at the Gentilly Landfill. It also provides information on the status of the Chef Menteur Landfill, an EPA disaster debris reduction pilot project in St. Bernard Parish, and a debris provision in the Water Resources Development Act of 2007. The review focused on EPA's and LDEQ's 2007 and 2008 debris-related Hurricane Katrina response activities in the New Orleans area.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: The report finds that debris management oversight relies on a Louisiana emergency order extended through August 29, 2008, EPA no action assurance letters covering asbestos requirements for government-ordered home demolitions, EPA's asbestos emissions monitoring plan, and LDEQ and EPA guidance. The emergency order broadens the state's definition of construction and demolition debris to include some potentially hazardous materials, and it is currently applicable to four named landfills in three parishes. The pace of home demolitions has been slow: LDEQ indicated that 12,000 FEMA-funded residence demolitions had been completed by February 2007, and FEMA estimated only another 5,000 had been completed by July 2008, with about 6,100 homes remaining. As of May 15, 2008, LDEQ had issued 120 enforcement actions for Katrina-related violations, including actions against five C&D landfills that received Katrina debris. An interagency effort called Operation Cleansweep inspected 178 sites in the Almonaster Corridor and referred 147 to LDEQ's enforcement division. At the Gentilly Landfill, LDEQ took actions that addressed many recommendations from a February 2006 draft report prepared for FEMA, including installing groundwater monitoring wells, surface water sampling ports, and inclinometers, and limiting daily and weekly debris intake. The Chef Menteur Landfill, opened in April 2006 and closed in August 2006, has not yet completed final closure activities and is awaiting a Corps of Engineers permit. An EPA disaster debris reduction pilot in St. Bernard Parish was redesigned to exclude regulated asbestos-containing material after community concerns and after EPA acknowledged an error in its risk estimate. A Water Resources Development Act provision restricting federal reimbursement for certain C&D debris disposal has not impacted debris disposal operations because EPA Region 6 determined that the types of waste under the emergency order seem consistent with what EPA identifies as material typically sent to a C&D landfill. The report makes no new recommendations in this review.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: In 2005, Hurricane Katrina resulted in more than 1,600 deaths and drove more than a million people from their homes. FEMA estimated in July 2008 that it had funded about 16,900 home demolitions, with an estimated 6,100 homes remaining to be demolished around the New Orleans area. It is estimated that more than 100 million cubic yards of disaster debris will have been generated when demolition and renovation are completed, more than twice the amount generated in 1992 by Hurricane Andrew. LDEQ indicated that 12,000 FEMA-funded residence demolitions had been completed by February 2007, and 17 months later, by July 2008, only another 5,000 had been completed. FEMA estimated that as of July 25, 2008, approximately 16,900 residences in Jefferson, Orleans, Plaquemines, St. Bernard, and St. Tammany Parishes had been demolished with FEMA funding since February 2006. EPA and LDEQ conducted 3,364 landfill observations at 13 landfill and debris storage or staging sites since October 2005. From October 2005 through May 2008, the observation counts were: Chef Menteur C&D landfill, 89; Empire Pit C&D landfill, 140; Gentilly C&D landfill, 699; Highway 90 C&D landfill, 755; Industrial Pipe C&D landfill, 125; Jefferson Parish Type I-II landfill, 38; Killona C&D landfill, 28; River Birch Type I-II landfill, 136; St. Bernard temporary debris storage and reduction site #1 (Paris Road Landfill), 232; St. Bernard temporary debris storage and reduction site #2 (Old Asphalt Plant), 54; Slidell C&D landfill, 616; Stranco C&D landfill, 143; Tidewater Sanitary / Coast Guard Road C&D landfill, 309; total, 3,364. LDEQ and EPA have observed demolition activities at 8,706 residences since March 2006; LDEQ conducted 1,109 observations from March 27, 2006, through October 20, 2006, and EPA conducted 7,597 demolition observations from October 21, 2006, through July 2008. EPA also conducted 828 floor tile demolition observations through July 2008. EPA has monitored for asbestos emissions at 300 of the 1,253 demolitions conducted under EPA's no action assurance letters, between August 6, 2007, and May 15, 2008. EPA officials told GAO that 1 out of 1,170 samples taken from over 300 demolition sites exceeded EPA's health-screening level for asbestos concentrations, but LDEQ officials said this instance was caused by a misinterpretation of the sampling analysis results and none of the samples exceeded EPA's health-screening levels; EPA confirmed that the one sample result in question was deemed inconclusive due to excessive particulate on the sample filter. The asbestos monitoring plan calls for monitoring a minimum of 10 percent of FEMA-funded demolitions of houses known to have, or assumed to have, regulated asbestos-containing material. As of May 15, 2008, LDEQ had issued 120 enforcement actions for Hurricane Katrina-related violations: 51 involved issues cutting across LDEQ's air, water, solid waste, or hazardous waste programs; 53 involved only solid waste, hazardous waste, or water; 9 were under the state's expedited penalties process; and 7 were air-related actions addressing regulated asbestos-containing material violations. In March and April 2007, agencies inspected 178 sites in the Almonaster Corridor and referred 147 to LDEQ's enforcement division. The Gentilly administrative order specified that daily debris intake shall not exceed 50,000 cubic yards, that weekly intake of uncompacted C&D waste be limited to 210,000 cubic yards initially and gradually increased to 280,000 cubic yards, and that debris be dumped until it reaches an elevation of no more than 25 feet. Gentilly was receiving about 6,000 to 7,000 cubic yards of debris each day. The order called for installation of 10 inclinometers, 11 groundwater monitoring wells, and 3 surface water sampling ports. LDEQ is testing groundwater for 62 chemicals, including arsenic, benzene, and lead, and surface water for 9 chemicals. Quarterly sampling results were within normal ranges with the exception of seven metals in groundwater samples and one metal in surface water samples, and LDEQ officials attributed the metal levels to surrounding soil sediment, which naturally contains metals such as lead at levels of around 15 to 20 parts per million. The Chef Menteur Landfill was opened under emergency authority in April 2006, closed in August 2006, and underwent comprehensive testing in November 2007; none of the air samples exceeded state or federal regulations. The initial emergency order was applicable to 25 of the state's 64 parishes, and the February 2008 emergency order covers five parishes: Jefferson, Orleans, Plaquemines, St. Bernard, and St. Tammany. EPA no action assurance letters have reduced by 2 or 3 days the time required to demolish homes.

recommended.name: What is recommended or required
recommended.text: This report makes no recommendations based on the work conducted for this review. It notes that GAO made six recommendations in its 2007 Hurricane Katrina report and encourages EPA to expeditiously complete its responses to all of those recommendations, which are aimed at minimizing environmental risks from future disasters and providing environmental health risk information to the public that is timely, complete, clear, and consistent. The report also encourages EPA to carefully consider the continued need to waive certain aspects of the Clean Air Act's asbestos requirements for building demolitions and to work with LDEQ as it considers whether it is necessary to continue to allow carpeting and furniture into some C&D landfills.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The report states that LDEQ officials said in July 2008 that the agency would likely continue to reauthorize the expanded C&D debris definition for some landfills beyond August 29, 2008, under an amended state emergency order, and that the order's extension says the need for an additional extension will be evaluated by the order's expiration date. EPA had not yet provided information on its responses to four of the six recommendations from GAO's 2007 report. LDEQ expected to complete an overall summary of the Operation Cleansweep effort by the end of the summer of 2008. As of the end of May 2008, the Corps of Engineers had not provided a time frame for issuance of the Clean Water Act permit needed before final closure of the Chef Menteur Landfill, and several pending lawsuits could affect the nature and timing of the landfill closure. GAO did not evaluate the technical merits of the February 2006 draft report on the Gentilly Landfill or the effectiveness of LDEQ's responses. LDEQ officials said they disagreed with, and had not taken action to respond to, the draft report's recommendations regarding landfill gas monitoring. At the Gentilly Landfill, sampling results were within normal ranges except for seven metals in groundwater samples and one metal in surface water samples; LDEQ attributed the metals to surrounding soil sediment and said it would continue to analyze results to develop baseline data. EPA acknowledged that an error in its risk estimate of the potential health effects of exposure to asbestos was a factor in the decision to exclude regulated asbestos-containing material from the revised St. Bernard Parish pilot project. FEMA questioned whether federal agencies could become liable for cleanup costs if the Gentilly Landfill became a Superfund site; EPA concluded that there is no way to protect against future Superfund liability absolutely.

about.name: What this document is about
about.text: This document is a September 2008 GAO report to congressional committees on aviation security, specifically TSA's oversight of domestic air carriers' preboarding checks of passengers against the No Fly and Selectee lists for domestic flights. It covers TSA's security-directive requirements, the extent of TSA's compliance testing, the April 2008 revision to the No Fly List security directive, and TSA's expectation that Secure Flight will be the ultimate solution. It is the public version of a restricted report, GAO-08-453SU.

findings.name: Key findings
findings.text: GAO found that TSA had issued two security directives requiring domestic air carriers to match passenger information to the No Fly and Selectee lists within 24 hours of scheduled departure but no later than check-in, and that before the April 2008 revision these directives were broad and did not specify how many or what types of name variations air carriers had to compare. The 14 air carriers GAO interviewed reported varied approaches to similar-name matching, so a passenger could be identified as a match by one carrier and not another. TSA had conducted limited testing of similar-name matching until a January 2008 special emphasis inspection of 83 air carriers found that no air carrier succeeded in identifying matches involving all types of name variations. TSA then revised the No Fly List security directive in April 2008 to establish a baseline similar-name-matching capability and planned a similar revision to the Selectee List security directive. TSA officials stated the baseline is an interim solution and Secure Flight is the longer-term solution. In fiscal year 2007, TSA found air carriers in compliance in 1,133 of 1,145 watch-list-related inspections, or 99 percent, but testing of similar-name matching was limited and inspectors acted without baseline evaluation criteria. A May 2008 special emphasis assessment of seven air carriers' compliance with the revised directive was classified but characterized by TSA as positive. GAO states it is too early to determine how TSA will assess compliance moving forward because its efforts are still underway.

numbers.name: Numbers that matter
numbers.text: According to TSA's Office of Intelligence, for the 3-year period January 2005 through December 2007, there were known incidents in which individuals on the No Fly List boarded international flights to or from the United States because of domestic air carriers' watch-list-matching failures. GAO interviewed officials from 14 domestic air carriers, which accounted for approximately 70 percent of passengers who boarded domestic flights in 2005; the results are not generalizable to all domestic air carriers. As of January 2008, 9 principal security inspectors oversaw domestic air carriers; the No Fly and Selectee list security directives applied to 72 domestic air carriers in fiscal year 2007. As of June 2008, 681 transportation security inspectors were responsible for 459 commercial airports. In fiscal year 2007, TSA conducted 1,145 watch-list-related inspections: 1,109 by transportation security inspectors at airports and 36 by principal security inspectors at corporate security offices; these covered 60 of the 72 carriers, and TSA found compliance in 1,133 inspections, or 99 percent. Documentation of name-matching tests appeared in 55 of 1,109 airport inspections and 6 of 36 corporate inspections; 6 of 9 principal security inspectors said their assessments had not included testing basic similar-name comparisons. In the air-carrier interviews, 10 of 14 carriers said more similar-name comparisons produce more potential matches, and 12 of 14 said large numbers of potential matches can cause congestion and longer waits. TSA's January 2008 special emphasis inspection lasted 3 days, tested 83 air carriers, 52 domestic and 31 foreign, using 100 No Fly List names, and found no air carrier successful in identifying matches involving all name-variation types. TSA conducted a special emphasis assessment in June, July, and September 2005 that tested exact-name matching only. A special emphasis assessment was conducted during May 20-29, 2008, of 7 air carriers' compliance with the revised No Fly List security directive; its details are classified. TSA expected Secure Flight to begin assuming watch-list matching for domestic flights in early calendar year 2009, and plans to deploy it beginning in January 2009. TSA estimated air carriers would need 2 to 4 weeks to implement the revised directive's requirements, while third-party vendor solutions could take almost 2 years.

recommended.text: The document makes no recommendations.

unsettled.name: What the document does not settle
unsettled.text: The document states that GAO could not determine the extent to which domestic air carriers may be failing to identify watch-listed individuals on domestic flights, because U.S. Customs and Border Protection does not screen domestic passengers and no second comparison occurs. GAO's interviews with 14 air carriers were not generalizable to all domestic air carriers, and GAO did not independently verify each carrier's reported method of implementation. GAO determined that the sampling and procedures for TSA's 2005 special emphasis assessment were insufficient for a reliable estimate of success rates, and GAO did not assess the reliability of TSA's January 2008 special emphasis inspection data or the May 2008 special emphasis assessment data. GAO did not independently analyze whether the new baseline is sufficient, and TSA could not provide data or analysis to support its assertion that requiring comparisons beyond the baseline was not warranted. The May 2008 assessment details are classified, so only TSA's general characterization as positive is public. TSA acknowledged the baseline does not address all name-variation vulnerabilities. The document says it is too early to determine the extent to which TSA will assess carriers' compliance going forward because corrective efforts were still underway as of early September 2008, and TSA's revised inspection handbook had not yet been released.

audience.name: Who it is for
audience.text: This report is addressed to the congressional committees listed in the report, including the Senate Committees on Appropriations, Commerce, Science, and Transportation, Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs, and the Judiciary, and the House Committees on Appropriations, Homeland Security, Oversight and Government Reform, and Transportation and Infrastructure, to support congressional oversight of TSA's watch-list-matching oversight and the Secure Flight program.
